Badenoch says using amputee athletes to justify cutting disability benefits was ‘message of hope’

Good morning. At PMQs yesterday Andy Burnham said that Kemi Badenoch should withdraw the “double amputees run marathons” comment that she used to justify the Tory plan to cut sickness and disability benefits by £14bn. It was “crass and insensitive” , he said.

This morning Badenoch defended what she was saying claimed that, in fact, she was delivering a “message of hope”.

In an interview on the Today programme, asked if she accepted that her remark was insensitive, Badenoch said she didn’t. She went on:

double quotation mark I will speak the truth and I will say what I believe is common sense. And what I know is that, if people can work, then we should encourage them to work. And what I’m saying is actually a message of hope, that if people even with significant, problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work.

When the presenter, Nick Robinson , put it to her that it was unreasonable to use an exceptional case as a guide to what most disabled people should be doing, Badenoch did not agree. “We do use extreme examples to illustrate things,” she said.

Robinson tried again, saying she was taking “one extreme case [to] imply that anybody on disability benefits should just get on with it”. Badenoch accused him of “faux outrage” and “tone policing”. She added:

double quotation mark People are free to disagree, but they know where I’m coming from. I will post more from the interview shortly.

Today the news will be dominated by two summits. This afternoon Burnham is in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. We have coverage of this on our Europe live blog.

And in China, Vladimir Putin, who invaded Ukraine, Xi Jinping, his leading ally, and Donald Trump , who is seen by many as a closet Putin ally, are meeting now. You can read about that here.

We will have comments open in about an hour. That is because I will be doing a Q&A this afternoon, probably from about 3pm, and I will try to answer as many questions as possible. Do post them below the line.

Here is the agenda for the day.

9.30am: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister, takes questions in the Commons.

10am: The Conservative party announces the results of the first round of voting in the election of its candidate for London mayor for 2028. James Cleverly , the former home secretary and former foreign secretary, is expected to get more than 50% of the vote, meaning a second round of voting should not be necessary.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Noon: Heather Hallett, the Covid inquiry chair, publishes her report on the test, trace and isolate system.

Around 12.15pm (UK time): Andy Burnham arrives in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. He is expected to speak to the media later in the afternoon after the plenary has finished.

1pm: Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, attends a meeting of the British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference in Dublin.

Jenrick widely mocked after criticising 'deep scar' left by Thatcher's policies - despite naming his daughter after her

Robert Jenrick has been mocked and criticised after giving an interview critical of Margaret Thatcher.

At the Conservative party conference just two years ago, before he defected to Reform UK, Jenrick astonished party members by revealing that, such was his admiration for the former PM, he had burdened one of his daughters with Thatcher as a middle name .

Even by Tory standards that was seen as excessive – although Thatcher is probably the only former party leader, other than Winston Churchill, who has always been venerated by the vast majority of its embers.

Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, was also a huge Thatcher admirer in the 1980s, and he only left the Conservative party after she was ousted and John Major signed the Maastricht Treaty.

But Reform UK are now polling well in former Labour seats in the Midlands and the north of England and Jenrick’s comments about Thatcher seem to be part of a deliberate tilt to appeal to this audience.

In an interview with the Sun , Jenrick said:

double quotation mark I grew up in the Black Country, and my mum and dad worked in heavy industry and those industries were destroyed in the 1970s by out-of-control trade unions , bad management, and by the policies that Labour and Tory governments pursued at that time. And yeah, the Thatcher government turned that around. But they also did it in a way which left a deep scar on these communities. Businesses went under. There was a loss of pride and identity which has taken a long time and perhaps has never fully recovered.

Jenrick also criticised Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, for “wrapping herself in the mantle of Margaret Thatcher ”. Pointing out that Burnham also defines himself in relation to Thatcher (the PM argues that many of the problems facing Britain now started with policies she introduced), Jenrick said Westminster should “move on” and talk about the future. He said:

double quotation mark Margaret Thatcher is as dated a reference to my kids as Winston Churchill was to me when I was growing up, and that doesn’t feel that long ago.

In a post on social media, Luke Tryl , the More in Common pollster, said that disowning Thatcherism was a logical electoral strategy for Reform UK.

double quotation mark Further evidence I think Reform is leaning into where their actual potential voter pool actually is and if you’re not going to be able to squeeze affluent Tories, your voter pool of socially conservative/economically statist voters dont want Thatcherism 2.0

But Jenrick has also been widely mocked for his comments, which will do nothing to quell claims that – even by MP standards – he is a shameless opportunist.

Quite what Jenrick’s daughter thinks of this all remains a mystery. However, the Tories have issued a comment. A Conservative spokesperson said:

double quotation mark Whether it’s Brexit, the border or the Iron Lady, Robert Jenrick’s political compass is all over the place. Having named his daughter after Margaret Thatcher, Bobbie now wants to disown her. You cannot believe a word he says. He has no fixed principles, no convictions and no consistency. He is a political weather vane, pointing whichever way he thinks the wind is blowing. It is impossible to keep up with which version of Robert Jenrick will turn up next.

UK to give Ukraine 1,000 long-range strike drones

Andy Burnham is going to announce details of a £260m package of support for Ukraine at the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin this afternoon. It will include more than 1,000 long-range strike drones. No 10 says:

double quotation mark Arriving in Berlin today, Andy Burnham is set to announce a new £260m package, including long-range drones, which can travel more than 1000km - the equivalent to the distance between London and Berlin. The package will include strike drones able to carry heavy warheads capable of flattening targets in a single hit, enabling Ukraine to target military production facilities and other legitimate military targets far behind the front lines. The UK will also build and deliver vital maritime, logistical, and surveillance drones to allow Ukraine to resupply front line forces, ensuring stocks such as blood and fridges for medical stores reach those on the front line … Today’s announcement of further support won’t just boost Ukraine’s front lines; it will also bring jobs and opportunity around the country, with more than 80% of this funding to be spent in the UK – including with small and medium-sized businesses across Wales, Northern Ireland, and Scotland.

Leaseholders in England and Wales to have ground rent capped in 2028

Matthew Pennycook , the housing minister, was doing an interview round this morning to promote the news that the government is publishing its leasehold reform bill today. Under the plans, leaseholders in England and Wales will have their ground rent capped in 2028. Kiran Stacey has the details.

Labour has issued this statement about James Cleverly being selected as the Tory candidate for London mayor. It is from Bridget Phillipson , the Labour chair.

double quotation mark James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London. He backed a no deal Brexit and Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services, and opposed action to clean up London’s air. Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital. They deserve a better future, not a return to the same old Tory failure.

UK must decide whether it wants to be or not to be in EU, says Rosencrantz at EU summit

Jakub Krupa writes the Guardian’s Europe live blog.

Over in Brussels, EU ministers are arriving for foreign affairs talks, with questions already popping up about tomorrow’s EU-UK summit , 10 years on from Britain’s vote to leave the bloc.

Ireland’s EU minister Thomas Byrne said the main areas to be discussed on Friday “will have very significant benefits” for all parties, with the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement set to resolve “one of the biggest problems out of Brexit”.

But he was cautious talking about the future relationship with the EU, saying that while he had “no doubt that the EU and Britain will want to go further on that path, we have seen how complex even dealing with the issues for tomorrow is and how long it takes.”

Sweden’s Jessica Rosencrantz stressed it is “up to the citizens of the UK to decide how close you want to work with the EU”.

But, again, asked if Britain could rejoin the bloc and keep its historical opt-outs and rebates, she dismissed it as “a highly speculative question”. She added:

double quotation mark Let’s remember how the discussion was at the time of Brexit. In that light, I think it is amazing that we now can have a big summit together, with discussions on how we can come closer together when it comes to trade and mobility.

Poland’s EU minister Ignacy Niemczycki said Warsaw’s approach “has always been very pragmatic,” as he stressed that the EU after Brexit is “weaker.” He said:

double quotation mark I would like us, wherever possible, to work out such mechanisms so it works for both of us. … This is a country that thinks similarly to us in Europe on many issues and there is no reason for us to treat each other like enemies. We are friends and let’s find the right formula for that.

In a cheeky comment, he added:

double quotation mark I would encourage everyone to think seriously about the benefits of being in the EU, … and I think the people of the UK see it [too], now that they are outside the union.

Tories choose James Cleverly as their candidate for London mayor in 2028

James Cleverly has been selected as the Conservative party’s candidate for the next London mayoral election.

The former foreign secretary and former home secretary won 86% of the votes in the ballot, beating Westminster councillor Festus Akinbusoye and former parliamentary candidate Sara Gezdari. A fourth candidate, communications professional Alex Challoner, was eliminated before the shortlist was drawn up for the ballot.

The next election for London mayor will take place in 2028.

Cleverly said he was “all in” for the race and would not be seeking reselection as an MP. He represents Braintree in Essex.

After the result was announced, Cleverly said the current mayor, Labour’s Sadiq Khan, was letting London down. He said:

double quotation mark People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place, businesses, job creators, families leaving London, and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related. The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. When I ask Londoners, do you feel safe walking home at night? The answer is no. It’s shameful, it’s a failure, and it’s not just crime. We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the second world war and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London.

Congratulating Cleverly, Kemi Badenoch said London was in decline and Labour was to blame.

Any questions for Andrew Sparrow?

This afternoon I will be answering questions from readers. Please post your questions below the line (comments are open today), and I will be answering from about 3pm until 5pm, or a bit later.

This is the latest in a regular Conversations series where Guardian journalists answer questions from readers. I last did one in April .

Please feel free to ask about anything related to British politics. I will try to answer as many as I can, but in particular I will focus on a) the ones that seem most interesting and b) the ones where I think I might have something sensible to say.

Tulip Siddiq says she is considering legal action against former Bangladesh leader

The former minister Tulip Siddiq has said she is considering taking legal action against the former interim leader of Bangladesh over corruption allegations made by his administration led her to resign from the UK government last year, Alexandra Topping reports.

In her Today programme interview, Kemi Badenoch said that she was “worried” by the idea of the government intervening to get the Russell Brand prison message video removed from YouTube. (See 10.04am .) She said that, while Brand had been convicted, his wife (who posted the video) was a separate person.

Badenoch said:

double quotation mark My personal opinion is that Russell Brand has been convicted. He is guilty under the law. The rule of law applies to everyone in this country. His wife is a separate person. She can make the protestations that she likes. I’m very concerned if people in prison are able to use other conduits to be able to send messages. I think that that is unorthodox. But YouTube is a private platform. I think that immediately demanding the private platforms take things down without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from. If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I’m quite worried about government intervening.

During his interview round this morning, Matthew Pennycook said the Ministry of Justice is in “dialogue” with Google as it tries to get the tech firm to take down the Russell Brand video. (See 10.04pm .)

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said:

double quotation mark It is only right that the government asks for content that is distressing for victims to be taken down and we strongly believe YouTube should remove this content. Removal ultimately depends on the platform’s own terms.

Meta disabled Brand’s Instagram and Facebook accounts after his conviction, the Press Association reports.

A Google spokesperson said:

double quotation mark We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube Partner Programme in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.

Minister admits government cannot force Google to remove Russell Brand prison video from YouTube

The government has no power to make Google take down a YouTube video with a message from Russell Brand from prison claiming he is innocent of his crimes, a minister has admitted.

As Nadeem Badshah reports, the government has asked Google to take down the video.

Google has reportedly denied the request because it determined its rules had not been broken, the Press Association reports.

Asked about this in an interview on BBC Breakfast this morning, Matthew Pennycook , the housing minister, said:

double quotation mark We don’t have any power to mandate a removal of content. That is up to Google. It’s based on their terms and conditions. But as I’ve been very clear, we’ve made a request in this instance because we feel very strongly that victims shouldn’t have to see this content. We hope they do so because they have taken action on their platform before. They banned, for example in 2023, Russell Brand for making money off the platform because his off-platform behaviour was seen to cause harm.

BAE to slash 1,000 jobs across head office and air business to streamline orders

BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, triggering calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor , Lauren Almeida and Jasper Jolly report.

Badenoch says it's 'disturbing' that Xi, Trump and Putin look like they're 'trying to carve up world between them'

Alexandra Topping is a Guardian political correspondent.

Kemi Badenoch was in a straight-talking mode on the media round this morning, calling the historic meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin “disturbing”, saying it looked like they were trying to “carve” up the world” between them.

Speaking on the Today programme, the leader of the opposition said the meeting was “absolutely not reassuring”.

She said:

double quotation mark There are three world leaders who look like they’re trying to carve up the world between them, a tri-polar world where Xi gets Asia, America gets the western hemisphere and Russia gets Europe, and that is very concerning, especially seeing Donald Trump call President Putin his friend. Russia is not America’s friend, it certainly hasn’t been during my lifetime. But also at a time when we’re all worried about where the Ukraine war is going, the message that is sending to President Zelensky and of course the other summit that is taking place … is very concerning indeed. And what I want to know is where we fit in in all of this. I don’t want to be in a polarised world run by Russia. I’ll do everything I can to make sure that doesn’t happen.

Badenoch went further than the prime minister, who was asked about the meeting by Ed Davey at prime minister’s questions yesterday. The Liberal Democrat leader said “the security implications of Trump, Putin and Xi cosying up” should highlight the need for a fresh deal with the European Union.

Burnham replied that he would be in Berlin for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing to support Ukraine in China, but stopped short of expressing concern about the meeting of the three world leaders.

He said:

double quotation mark The thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine and that is what this government will do. And on this issue, I do pay tribute to all sides of the house because that is what we’ve managed to do in the years since the conflict began and that is the right thing to do … Let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in [China] – this country is squarely with Ukraine.

stories.title: Ted Cruz-led committee approves Trump FCC nominee 15-0 as Democrats boycott vote
stories.summary: Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.

A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.

All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing.

Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then seek require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.

Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.”

Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.”

False testimony allegation

At a hearing last week, Thumann said she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?”

“It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.”

The FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters.

Thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.”

Emails touched on 60 Minutes complaints

Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann.

Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes , and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages.

The emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding.

“Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?”

Democrats aimed to prevent quorum

Democrats announced yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell said in a statement.

Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said.

Cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session.

Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today.

In the Standing Rules of the Senate , paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.”

While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.”

Cruz rejects paired nominations

FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz said that’s not a requirement.

“There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz said during the Republican-only meeting.

The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It says, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”

Republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term.

“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week.

stories.title: Elon Musk says record $446m spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
stories.summary: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.

Published 19 November 2026, 01:56 GMT

Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.

Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.

Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.

The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.

Musk was speaking virtually , external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.

"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.

He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."

This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.

"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

Musk has worn a Maga hat in public on several occasions

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings , as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.

Kristalina Georgieva says countries needed to be ready for tech rollout, adding: ‘You snooze, you lose’

Business live – latest updates

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.

“This call for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen , Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Central banks have been forced to raise interest rates this year after the outbreak of war in February drove the global oil price above $100 a barrel, reigniting inflationary pressures around the world. The European Central Bank raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, followed by the US Federal Reserve in September and the Bank of England earlier this month .

Financial markets expect further increases in the cost of borrowing next year, as the rapid rollout of AI bolsters economic growth against the volatile backdrop of the conflict.

However, global oil prices have fallen back in recent weeks, following the US midterm elections and an upswing in the supply of crude . Fears about an AI bubble and febrile conditions in global equity markets could dent business investment, and economists warn of a slowdown in demand as high inflation squeezes households.

Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is forever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”

stories.title: The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
stories.summary: Many of the names and arguments that defined the Brexit period are emerging again, as the debate over the UK being part of the EU is back on the agenda.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 hour ago

"Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce.

It's a lyric Brexit veterans might be humming to themselves this week. Maybe even the prime minister, who is an avid fan of the Manchester band.

Some of the names - and arguments - that defined the Brexit period inside and outside Parliament are starting to emerge again, as the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU returns.

"It's like déjà vu with knobs on," said one veteran of the Leave campaign to us.

A new group called Stay Out has been set up, backed by figures who were part of the official Leave campaign in 2016. Boris Johnson has been back in the headlines, saying he still thinks Britons would choose to be outside the bloc.

Pro-EU groups such as the European Movement are raising their voices, pointing to the range of politicians, diplomats and academics they have supporting their argument. And a steady stream of Labour figures are now emerging to say they want to rejoin.

The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy made the argument on the BBC on Wednesday , saying Labour should go into the next election backing renegotiating membership of the EU and then putting that to people in another referendum.

He joins a list of cabinet ministers under Sir Keir Starmer who want to revisit EU membership; a list that includes former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, former Business Secretary Peter Kyle and former Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens. Others who served around Sir Keir's cabinet table think the same privately.

That is significant. Yes, they all backed Remain in 2016. But these are figures who were part of a government elected on a manifesto saying it was important to make Brexit work.

They set red lines in that manifesto because they thought the public had moved on. But they have now decided to say - most of them very publicly - that they think the picture has changed and the UK needs to think again.

The prime minister has opened the door to all options, from single market membership to rejoining the customs union to a referendum on full membership.

But in recent days, his language has softened a little from the clear commitment in his party conference speech that around the time of this Friday's summit he would "lay out to the country" the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with Brussels.

After some confusion about when this would take place, the government now says this will happen around the time that Burnham presents his 10-year plan, right before Parliament's Christmas break.

Burnham's allies say this will allow him to tie his EU policy more closely to his domestic agenda, arguing that a different arrangement with Europe would help with his other priorities such as the cost of living and re-industrialisation.

Others worry that the all-consuming nature of the EU debate means that it will drown out the other parts of the 10-year plan.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: 'Hard Brexit we were given not good enough for Britain,' says Burnham

What remains unclear is the timeframe for the process that will follow Burnham setting out what he sees as the different Brexit options.

The prime minister has always been clear that Labour's commitments in its 2024 manifesto not to rejoin the single market or the customs union - let alone the EU altogether - still stand until the next general election.

And it was to those manifesto red lines that Burnham returned when asked about rejoining the EU at PMQs on Wednesday.

Yet those would not preclude Burnham initiating negotiations now on an arrangement breaking those red lines, which would take effect after the next general election.

Nevertheless, some on the prime minister's own side ponder that - having turned the volume up on the whole issue this autumn - he might be wise to turn it down a little in the new year, so it doesn't risk drowning out other things ministers want to talk about.

Andy Burnham is a prime minister who likes to explore things out loud. It's part of what he sees as a new way of doing politics, where he answers questions honestly and is prepared to discuss ideas while they are being formed, not just after they are a settled position.

It is a style that seeks to present a sense of a desired direction, even if some of the specifics end up being walked back from.

But even though it might be some time before the government has an official position on the future relationship, plenty of people are discussing what might happen next.

"It is all go again! My inbox is full of the same old stuff I thought I'd seen the back of years ago," one senior figure told us.

There are some nerves in the Labour Party about what might happen next. MPs who we have spoken to hold a range of views, which shows why this won't be plain-sailing.

Some are worried about re-opening the debate, calling it "toxic".

Others worry that the prime minister could disappoint pro-EU voters if he doesn't go far enough.

Others still wonder if the argument has changed enough that voters would decide differently in a new referendum.

"Both sides need fresh arguments, not the ones we all got tired of last time," said one.

"If this just looks like politicians wanting to rejoin because they never got over leaving then it's dead on arrival.

"If we can show that actually this is being led by businesses, by farmers, by different parts of society who need to rejoin because of the ways Brexit has harmed them, then it's a different matter," said another.

And what would the new EU the UK could rejoin look like?

Some Labour MPs ponder that the EU is changing – with the possibility of more right-wing leaders at the top table. They question whether they would want to be part of that.

Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship Published 1 day ago

The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left Published 1 day ago

UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham says ahead of EU summit Published 2 days ago

A long standing diplomat from an EU member state said that the possibility of political change within the EU, alongside the recent offer of associate membership to Canada and at least the possibility of a potential future arrangement with Ukraine after any peace deal, could mean Brussels becomes more open to looser forms of membership that it has not been willing to consider before.

But then there is Scotland. If the government backs another EU vote, some Scottish MPs worry it adds to the argument for another vote on Scottish independence.

Despite the warnings, plenty of MPs are delighted that the Europe debate is back on the agenda.

One summed it up like this: "It doesn't really matter to me at this point where the PM is heading on this – it's all good for appealing to progressive voters. Just being seen to talk about this even without it necessarily being clear what we're going to do is a big change from before."

That seems to be a prevailing mood at the moment. Lots of Labour MPs are happy the EU debate is back. But not all of them.

Andy Burnham will on Friday sign a new deal with the EU which ministers believe will drive economic growth and cut red tape for British businesses. It will be heralded as a new moment for the relationship.

But how much further could the reset go?

The government hasn't decided yet - but plenty of others have their own views.

stories.title: Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick
stories.summary: "This time requires leadership and fortitude," Senator Bill Cassidy said.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“This time requires leadership and fortitude,” Senator Bill Cassidy said.

In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation.

Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy’s decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats.

In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA’s current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn’t say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is “quite lethal” or that children are given vaccine doses the “size of a soda bottle.” Overton repeatedly refused to answer whether Trump could ever be wrong.

Axios quoted a senior Trump administration official as saying that Overton’s nomination was dropped because she “lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation.”

The Senate’s Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, chaired by Bill Cassidy (R-La.), was scheduled to vote on Overton’s nomination Wednesday. In a social media post Tuesday night, after her nomination was withdrawn, Cassidy said he believed she had a “viable confirmation path.” But he said the nomination was “abandoned” after some anti-abortion senators sought commitments from her that they couldn’t get. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” Cassidy said.

“Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats,” Cassidy noted.

O’Neill canceled

After Overton’s last-minute withdrawal, the HELP committee’s agenda for Wednesday was updated again this morning to scrap a scheduled vote on Jim O’Neill, who was Trump’s nominee to run the NSF.

O’Neill has been criticized for lacking the science experience needed to run the foundation. In the past, O’Neill worked as a Silicon Valley investor and entrepreneur and became a close ally of Peter Thiel. But under Trump, O’Neill has been the deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services and served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. O’Neill took over the latter role after the former director, Susan Monarez, was ousted from it less than a month after her Senate confirmation. She later told Senators Kennedy fired her for refusing to blindly approve vaccine recommendations from his anti-vaccine advisors.

In remarks this morning , Cassidy said that O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from [Health] Secretary [Robert F.] Kennedy [Jr.].” As an example, Cassidy specifically referenced O’Neill’s role in the firing of Monarez. “Several members of the [HELP] committee had concerns regarding this,” Cassidy said.

“This time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy added.

The NSF has been hard hit by the Trump administration and actions by Elon Musk’s DOGE. The NSF has been forced to cancel hundreds of research grants and taken brutal cuts to its budget and staff in the past two years. In April, the Trump administration also terminated all members of the board that steers the NSF, called the National Science Board. Former members feared that it would make way for O’Neill to stack the board with political allies, pointing to how Trump filled the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology with tech billionaires —including leaders of Meta, Google, Oracle, and Nvidia—instead of top scientists and researchers.

stories.title: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work
stories.summary: Platform companies are luring doctors, lawyers, and Ph.D.s with top rates, but then use the same tactics of pay cuts and sudden ghosting that have plagued global data workers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ideas

Platform companies are luring doctors, lawyers, and Ph.D.s with top rates, but then use the same tactics of pay cuts and sudden ghosting that have plagued global data workers.

By Julián Posada

Julián Posada is an assistant professor at Yale University and the author of “Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence.”

Arguments, opinions and essays from a global perspective.

The gig economy has arrived for cardiologists. Recruiting platform Outlier, run by Scale AI, advertises offers of up to $180 an hour for physicians in the U.S. to design complex cardiac scenarios, review artificial intelligence-generated reports, and rank model outputs. The site offers up to $7.50 an hour for Tagalog work in the Philippines for the same job, and up to $12.50 an hour for Swahili in Tanzania.

Companies like Scale AI first outsourced data work to wherever labor was cheapest. Now, they are recruiting physicians, lawyers , and Ph.D.s to generate and annotate data, rank model answers, and verify outputs. Higher credentials can raise the advertised rate, but the platform still controls payment and working conditions.

They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on.

I’ve spent the last six years interviewing the people who do this work. Most were in Venezuela, where economic collapse has left a large, educated population online and out of options. One of them, Rogelio, taught computer science until the economic crisis and the pandemic left his family without work. His 13-year-old son discovered they could earn money labeling images of cars and roads on the platforms Hive and Scale AI’s Remotasks, using a laptop the Hugo Chávez government had issued to schoolchildren a decade earlier. The boy made 18 cents for a few hours of work. Rogelio joined him and made just over $2 on his first day.

For a while, the work paid. A task called Beast Mode where workers labeled objects in people’s homes paid more than any other work the family had done. In December 2020, with schools closed and the whole family working, it brought in $20 in a single day. It was the most they would ever make. By early 2021, Beast Mode had disappeared, and their earnings fell below Hive’s $5 weekly payout threshold.

This is how many platforms operate: They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on . Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and made a splash in Kenya the same year. In March 2024, it discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan. Scale AI attributed the closures to “enhanced security protocols,” and said notices had gone out three weeks ahead but later acknowledged that Kenyan workers never received them “due to operational errors.” Most workers who spoke to Rest of World at the time said the platform simply froze them out.

The pattern has a name, and it’s older than AI: extractivism. It is a system that takes resources and value from people and places for accumulation elsewhere, on terms set by the buyer rather than the worker. The term also stands for what is taken and what is left behind. The crisis that put Rogelio’s family online was the residue of an oil economy that built little else.

An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.

One woman I interviewed in Venezuela drew a pension from the state oil company. By 2021, it was worth about $1 a month, which she said couldn’t buy half a dozen eggs. She was labeling data on Hive to make up the difference, but that income was even less secure. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.

AI is usually described as built on extracted data: authors’ books , artists’ works , all used to train models. But the extraction has another layer: the new examples, evaluations, and corrections commissioned to improve those models. That material has to be created by someone, for a fee, which is set by the platform — whether it is $2 for the teacher in Venezuela or up to $180 an hour for a cardiologist in the U.S.

Outlier’s terms let the company delay or suspend payment during an investigation of a worker’s tasks and withhold “some or all amounts accrued” where it finds a violation “in the company’s sole determination.” The company may also deactivate an account “immediately without prior notice for any reason.” The same language appeared word for word in the Remotasks terms that Rogelio’s family worked under in 2021.

Earlier this year, Josh Dzieza reported on the laid-off lawyers , scientists , and screenwriters now filling these platforms. Of the more than 30 workers he interviewed, nearly all described the same arc: Demands increased, target times shrank, and pay fell as a project went on. One designer was tagging videos for Meta at $21 an hour when the project ended for “scope changes.” Days later, the same job reappeared under a new name at $16 an hour — the same sequence that Rogelio’s family went through five years earlier.

Of course, workers can leave, and many do. But the ones who stay are often those who can’t leave. One woman I interviewed was confined to her home during the Covid-19 pandemic by a health condition and couldn’t risk losing the job. “This is my only source of income,” she told me.

The rate can change suddenly, the task can disappear without warning, and they have no say over any of it.

None of this is unknown within the industry. In a 2024 meeting convened by the nonprofit Partnership on AI and the Fairwork project which rates platform companies, I sat with representatives of AI companies and the outsourcing firms that supply them. The AI companies said they didn’t employ the data workers; the outsourcing firms said their operations were determined by the prices the AI companies expected. Everyone agreed pay should be better, but when the question of representation came up, the room went quiet as no workers were present.

Workers have still acted. In March 2023, a judge in Kenya temporarily halted the dismissal of 260 Facebook content moderators, prevented Meta from moving their work to another contractor, and barred Meta and contractor Majorel from blacklisting workers. As workers fought in Kenya, Meta moved the work to West Africa.

American courts are also grappling with this issue. Claims by workers on Scale AI’s platforms led to a proposed settlement that has received preliminary approval in San Francisco. The company denies wrongdoing. A separate class action suit alleges Mercor misclassified more than 30,000 lawyers, doctors, and engineers while setting their pay and reviewing their work. Mercor’s clients have included OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, but they are not named as defendants. The case is ongoing.

A cardiologist who is offered a three-digit hourly rate is not in the same position as Rogelio and his family. What connects them is the fact that the rate can change suddenly, the task can disappear without warning, and they have no say over any of it.

The work will keep moving, and the rules will continue to be set by the companies that commission it, wherever the next worker logs on, whether in Kenya, Venezuela, or the Philippines.

Startups recalibrate Chinese AI for the West

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain

The founder’s stunning departure removes Beijing’s biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling, and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next.

The small African lab sounding the alarm on AI bioweapons

MinoHealth researchers in Ghana jailbroke their own LLM as a test. What emerged were thousands of toxin recipes—and an urgent push for regulation.

A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“H istoric” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.

Mr Xi looks like the power broker bringing Moscow and Washington together, and the gracious host, in a city which showcases China’s economic and technological progress and aspirations. The contrast between the glossy metropolis and a US currently beset by glaring tech failures hitting everything from flights to banking is especially flattering. For Mr Putin, who gloated about the “humiliation” of Europe in the run-up, this meeting is an even clearer win, making him look like a superpower peer rather than the leader of a pariah nation with a struggling economy.

Mr Trump has got a red carpet embrace, another “first” to promote – preferable to headlines dwelling on the Republicans’ midterms disaster – and the congenial company of strongmen. His nation has less to celebrate. Mr Trump seems to see meeting longstanding US allies as at best a chore. His bruising tariffs and nakedly transactional approach to security, as well as his love of autocrats, have pushed countries like the Philippines – which hosted the US president en route to China – into hedging their bets.

Mr Trump is not expected to raise Nvidia and suspected Chinese espionage – perhaps not least because his closeness to Jensen Huang, the company’s ousted CEO, makes the issue at least as discomfiting for him as it is for Beijing. The US president is unlikely to embarrass the two countries that are central to Iran’s ability to resist his disastrous and illegal war, or to press China over its facilitation of Russia’s war against Ukraine . Ukraine and Taiwan have reason to be anxious any time he speaks to Mr Putin and Mr Xi. But the US president is as likely to undermine them, whether deliberately or otherwise, in bilaterals or via a throwaway remark.

Comparisons to the 1945 Yalta summit of Joseph Stalin, Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill – which divided up Europe – grotesquely overstate the importance of a meeting scheduled to last less than an hour. Mr Xi does not do spontaneity, and is unlikely to be lured into sudden announcements. And despite the surface amity, the three still have strongly competing interests. China’s threat to rare earths brought a trade truce, but skirmishes continue. Mr Trump has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation . While China is arming itself at worrying speed, its arsenal is still dwarfed by those of the US and Russia.

Talking to rivals and adversaries is not inherently unwise. Under another US president, a closely focused and carefully prepared trilateral on, for instance, disarmament might even be fruitful. This is not that world. This will not be that meeting.

stories.title: Badenoch defends amputee marathon runners claim in benefits cut row
stories.summary: Paralympian Richard Whitehead had accused the Conservative leader of "weaponising" his sporting success.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 9 minutes ago

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has defended her suggestion that because double amputees run marathons more disabled people should work instead of claiming benefits.

Badenoch had used the example when setting out her party's plans to cut welfare spending by £36bn a year .

Her comments were criticised by Paralympian Richard Whitehead, who accused her of "weaponising" his sporting success, while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the Tory leader's words "crass and insensitive".

But in an interview with the BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Badenoch stood by the remarks, insisting that "if people even with significant problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work".

Asked if she accepted the comments were insensitive, Badenoch said: "No, no, no. I do not accept it. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense.

"What I know is that if people can work, then we should encourage them to work."

Badenoch acknowledged she had used "extreme examples to illustrate things", but added: "If someone can do that, then yes, your condition of ADHD or anxiety is mild."

"I will say things as they are. People may disagree with things that I say, and that's fine, this is a free country, people are free to disagree, but they know where I'm coming from," she said.

"I start from first principles: If you can work, you should work, and the Conservative Party is going to help you get a job."

Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation' Published 1 day ago

What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending? Published 29 October

In a speech setting out the Conservative Party's welfare plans last week, Badenoch said: "The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities even when they face serious challenges.

"Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world."

Responding to her speech, Whitehead - a double amputee marathon runner who has won four Paralympic medals - said he was "gobsmacked that somebody's sporting success would be weaponised in this way" , external .

In a post on social media , external , he also said: "Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day.

"The fact that some double-leg amputees can run marathons does not mean that disability support is unnecessary.

"Equally, the fact that some people with ADHD thrive despite limited support does not mean that others do not need meaningful assistance."

As part of their plans to cut welfare spending, the Conservatives have proposed stopping people from claiming disability benefits for "milder mental health issues and neurodiversity conditions such as anxiety, depression and ADHD", as well as "routine back and joint pain".

The party says its proposals to overhaul sickness and disability benefits would save £13.7bn a year.

It would also invest £1bn into health support, so people no longer eligible for cash benefits can access treatment to support their conditions instead.

stories.title: Security Council LIVE: Fragile Gulf calm tested as threats to Hormuz shipping mount
stories.summary: Nearly nine months after Israeli and US strikes on Iran set off a regional war, the Gulf remains on a knife edge. stories.title: Outage Chaos: When Tech is too Big to Fail
stories.summary: Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements. Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft , Apple *, banks , courts , airlines , and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication. As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally. There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug , negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. It’s a matter of public safety and economic stability that policymakers mitigate the impact of these disruptions before they occur. In order to do so, we must ensure antitrust prevents providers of key technical systems from becoming too big to fail. The harms inflicted by tech monopolies go beyond monetary costs to the end user. In fact, monopolists can often offer lower prices, or even offer free services, thanks to their greater scale and incentive to shut out competitors using free-flowing investment capital . The problem is this puts a few tech companies in a position of incredible influence. The true cost is a loss of control when our private data, access to knowledge, and free expression all become mediated by tools owned by a handful of billionaires. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. This isn’t just a bad deal for us as individuals. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. When everything from daily tasks to national security is reliant on a few digital monocultures , one mistake or exploit can cascade into an explosive impact. The risks multiply in the current investment climate, where financial markets reward companies that strip-mine redundancy and resiliency from critical systems. stories.title: Surveillance Isn't Safety: A Comic About Organizing Against Flock and Other Foes
stories.summary: In the new comic "Surveillance Isn't Safety"—available for free today— cartoonist Bryn Adams explores the growing movement against mass surveillance through their involvement in the community fight against Flock Safety in Cleveland, Ohio. It's a personal journey that will resonate widely with residents in hundreds of cities where communities are drawing the line against automated license plate readers (ALPRs). Jump to the Comic Or download the PDF Published in collaboration between EFF and Crucial Comix , Bryn's comic captures the authenticity of the grassroot backlash against the surveillance industry—undercutting Flock founder Garrett Langley's latest dubious defense that public opposition of his company's product isn't real. At the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference this fall, Langley accused the anti-surveillance activism of being driven by Russian bots and as being "inorganic." He pointed to the fact that many local groups were using similar language in their protest signs as supposed proof, when in reality, shared slogans are one of the hallmarks of a social movement. This was all misdirection from the grim realities that Flock and other ALPR systems facilitate: the mistakes are real; the abuse is real; the racism is real; and the targeting of dissenters , migrants , and abortion seekers is real. And, importantly, the cancelled contracts are real. Bryn's comic sheds light on the real abuses and threats driving communities to mobilize against Flock, Axon, and other ALPR vendors. It shows that coast-to-coast activism doesn't happen overnight—any more than a comic appears out of thin air as a finished product. As advisors on the cartoon, EFF watched how Bryn's script evolved from rough sketches to penciled drawings, then to inked and shaded panels, mirroring how the long-running movement against mass surveillance has steadily snowballed over the last few years. There is nothing “inorganic” about either: Both are built on passion, commitment, and putting in the work. stories.body:
About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users

At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined.

About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator .

In February 6.3% of households had someone using GLP-1 drugs, rising to 8.5% in August. Weight-loss pills such as Wegovy were approved in the UK in June. Patients previously had to use the injectable version.

Pills now account for more than one in 10 (11.2%) of GLP-1 users, while men are also driving the increase. Men make up just under a third (32%) of people taking weight-loss medication, up from 23% in February. Male users have nearly doubled to 830,000, up from 440,000 nine months ago.

The increased use of medications such as Mounjaro and Wegovy is causing people to buy less food at the supermarket and change their buying habits, according to a survey of more than 9,600 households.

In the year after starting to take the drugs, households with a GLP‑1 user collectively spent £1bn less on groceries than expected compared with similar households. In June, Worldpanel calculated the total saved by households with a GLP-1 user was £780m.

This represents 415m fewer items bought, or £389 a year displaced from the shopping baskets of households with a GLP-1 user, according to the research by Worldpanel, which has been tracking the effects of the drugs on buying behaviour since March 2024.

Nishita Pattni, a senior consultant for Worldpanel by Numerator, said: “In just six months, between February and August 2026, user numbers rose almost as much as they did in the whole of the previous year.

“For many people, a daily pill is far easier than an injection, and with the surge in male users, we only expect the appeal of these drugs to grow.”

GLP-1 users are now found in a similar percentage of households in Great Britain as those that buy popular branded products such as Kellogg’s Rice Krispies (8.6%) and Corona beer (8.4%).

People taking weight-loss medication were not simply buying fewer groceries, the research found. Spend and volume were falling at a similar rate, creating winners and losers.

after newsletter promotion

Products associated with indulgence, as well as impulse purchases, have taken the biggest hit.

Alcohol spend has fallen by 15% more among GLP-1 users than in households where no one uses GLP-1, while the spend on crisps has fallen by a similar percentage, as users tend to snack less.

Conversely, portion-controlled products are growing in popularity. There has been a 30% rise in the number of frozen ready-meals sold, and an increase in the volume and spend on hot chocolate and malt drinks as people who take weight-loss drugs continue to enjoy small treats.

Chantel Kennaugh, the head of public sector and nutrition for Worldpanel by Numerator, said estimates suggest that GLP-1 usage is likely to surpass 10% of households in Great Britain in 2027. “This is not a flash-in-the-pan trend, but a seismic change that requires retailers and manufacturers to rethink their strategies.”

stories.title: Crew unaware of risks before Mike Lynch's yacht Bayesian sank, say investigators
stories.summary: The vessel sank off the coast of northern Sicily, killing seven people including British tech tycoon Mike Lynch.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
There were 22 people on board the Bayesian at the time of the incident

Published 19 November 2026, 00:05 GMT

The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about critical safety risks that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.

British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.

Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.

"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas , 59.

Mike Lynch and his daughter Hannah both died when the Bayesian sank

Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."

Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184ft) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.

The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".

In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.

WATCH: Millionaire Superyacht: Why Ships Sink

In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.

With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).

The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.

The wreckage of the Bayesian off the coast of Porticello, Sicily

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.

Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.

They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.

The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.

Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.

As it heeled over, five people were injured, either by falling or by items falling on them and a deckhand was thrown into the sea, the report said.

As water started entering the yacht, two of the guests "used the furniture drawers as an improvised ladder to exit into the central alleyway", then climbed along the internal walls to get into the saloon.

The MAIB's final report into the sinking, published on Thursday, appeared to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecution experts have reportedly blamed errors by the crew rather than problems with the yacht.

The investigation was carried out alongside a criminal probe in Italy , where captain James Cutfield, chief engineer Tim Parker Eaton and deckhand Matthew Griffith are under investigation over potential charges of multiple manslaughter and culpable shipwreck.

British investigators said that Italian prosecutors had restricted access to some witnesses and evidence.

"It is possible that the circumstances depicted in this report may alter following disclosure of evidence withheld by the Italian authorities," the report says.

However, the MAIB's Graves said he was satisfied with the British investigation.

"We are content with our investigation, the investigation that we've undertaken, and the information we've used to feed into it."

The report also found that alcohol consumption had not contributed to the sinking.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

MAIB investigator Simon Graves: "This was an accident and there were a number of contributory factors"

The MAIB report makes seven recommendations to four agencies. It calls for new regulations to be set for single-hulled sailing vessels, and new rules around life rafts.

It also urges collaboration between the Met Office and its global counterpart to improve information-sharing of severe weather forecasts with mariners.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.
