stories.body:
Shining red light on your testicles or sitting in a sauna with an ice pack: social media has plenty of unusual suggestions for improving sperm quality.

This trend, sometimes called “spermmaxxing”, encourages men to take control of their reproductive health. As a reproductive scientist, I welcome that interest – I’ve even written a book about it . Male fertility has historically received less attention than women’s, and many men know surprisingly little about how their own bodies work.

But some spermmaxxing advice is based on experiments that tell us very little about someone’s actual chances of having a baby.

Listen to Michael Carroll speak about spermmaxxing on The Conversation Weekly podcast and on the Strange Health podcast.

A sperm count is only part of the picture. When scientists analyse semen, the fluid released during ejaculation, we examine how many sperm it contains, how many are alive and how well they swim. Their ability to move forwards is called progressive motility.

The World Health Organization’s reference figures include 39 million sperm per ejaculate and 30% moving forwards. These figures represent the lower end of results recorded among men whose partners conceived within a year. They are not a pass-or-fail fertility test.

Someone with a low sperm count may still conceive, while someone with millions of apparently healthy sperm may struggle. Pregnancy also depends on the egg and other stages of reproduction.

And, as my own research has shown , sperm can swim normally while carrying DNA damage that a routine test misses.

Do spermmaxxing hacks work?

Take red-light therapy. A laboratory study found that exposing sperm to particular wavelengths of red or near-infrared light improved their movement.

But shining light on sperm in a laboratory dish is very different from shining it on someone’s testicles. There is insufficient evidence that doing so improves fertility.

Then there are ice packs, sometimes promoted for use in saunas.

The testicles hang outside the body because sperm production works best at temperatures 2-4°C below normal body temperature. Research involving ten men found that regular sauna exposure temporarily impaired sperm production.

But putting ice against the scrotum, the pouch of skin containing the testicles, is not an established fertility treatment and risks injuring the skin. Avoiding prolonged excessive heat is a more sensible approach.

Abstinence advice is equally confusing. Some influencers suggest saving up sperm by avoiding ejaculation for long periods.

Longer gaps can increase the number of sperm in a sample, but an analysis of 13 clinical trials found that shorter periods of abstinence were associated with better forward movement and less DNA fragmentation – breaks in the genetic material carried by sperm.

This doesn’t mean ejaculating as frequently as possible will improve fertility. The optimal interval remains uncertain, and a change in sperm measurements does not necessarily translate into a greater chance of pregnancy.

Another misconception is that taking testosterone will help you produce more sperm.

The hormone is essential for sperm production, but taking testosterone supplements or anabolic steroids can suppress the signals from the brain telling the testicles to produce their own testosterone.

This can dramatically reduce sperm production , sometimes to zero. Production often recovers after treatment stops, but recovery can take months or longer.

Men considering testosterone treatment who want children should discuss fertility with their doctor beforehand.

What a sperm test can miss

Sperm need to carry healthy DNA, the genetic instructions passed from a father to a developing embryo.

In research my colleagues and I conducted , we exposed human sperm in the laboratory to compounds involved in glycation, chemical reactions between sugars and protein molecules.

One compound, glyoxal, increased a marker of oxidative DNA damage without significantly affecting how well the sperm swam.

This experiment does not prove that eating sugar causes infertility. It demonstrates why sperm counts and swimming ability cannot tell us everything about reproductive health.

And what about alarming claims that sperm counts are collapsing worldwide?

A large analysis published in 2023 reported substantial declines across studies spanning several decades.

However, a 2026 Danish study involving 8,320 men found relatively stable semen measurements between 1996 and 2022.

These studies examined different populations using different methods. The Danish findings do not disprove declines elsewhere, but they demonstrate why we need to examine geographical differences and study methods before drawing sweeping conclusions about global fertility.

What actually helps?

There is more reason to focus on general health than expensive fertility gadgets.

Smoking is associated with poorer semen quality . Research has also linked vaping with lower sperm counts, although it cannot establish that vaping carries the same reproductive risks as smoking.

A 2025 review found associations between Mediterranean-style diets, rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and olive oil, and some measures of better sperm quality. However, stronger evidence is needed to establish whether following this diet improves pregnancy rates.

Research also links disrupted sleep with poorer sperm quality . Exercise and maintaining a healthy weight can support reproductive health , although lifestyle changes cannot resolve every cause of infertility.

If conception is proving difficult, both partners should be assessed. The NHS recommends seeking medical advice after a year of trying, or sooner in certain circumstances.

Finally, sperm count is no measure of masculinity. Men experiencing infertility can face considerable isolation and shame, and turning sperm production into a competition risks making that worse.

Greater interest in male fertility is welcome. But improving reproductive health requires understanding what the science can tell us, recognising what remains uncertain and giving men access to reliable information rather than another miracle cure.

stories.body:
A surprising thing has happened at the UN climate conference, Cop31 , as it gears up to its conclusion in Antalya, Turkey. Negotiators are discussing how to cool the planet.

You might think this should not be surprising, but how to respond to the latest climate science was not on the agenda when the meeting started. It has been forced onto it by some of the countries most vulnerable to climate change – the small island states – in response to two alarming scientific reports in the last month.

The World Meteorological Organization has confirmed that the rate at which the Earth is heating up is accelerating . One reason is the planet is becoming less “reflective”: the loss of ice and snow, changes in cloud formation and (paradoxically) reductions in atmospheric pollution means that more solar radiation is being absorbed rather than reflected into space.

The result is that the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C will not be met. There’s a new term for this new warming trajectory: “overshoot”. As a United Nations Environment Programme (Unep) report explains, the best we can hope for now is to exceed 1.5°C but then limit the extent of the overshoot, peaking emissions as soon as possible and then returning to 1.5°C later in the century.

Unfortunately, Unep also notes that this may be easier said than done. The longer temperatures remain above 1.5°C, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible changes to systems such as polar ice sheets and glaciers, ocean currents and the Amazon rainforest, which could make returning to lower temperatures impossible.

Beyond cutting emissions

Up until now we have thought there were basically two responses to global heating. We needed to cut emissions (mitigation), and cope with the warming we experienced (adaptation). But overshoot means that achieving net zero emissions is not enough. By the time we get there the temperature will be too high.

Overshoot will require two other kinds of response. As well as cutting the flow of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, we can physically take them out, a process known as carbon dioxide removal or CDR.

We will need to consider different ways to increase the planet’s reflectivity. These include limiting aircraft contrails (which trap heat), expanding the white surface areas of the earth (both buildings and crops), or making glaciers more stable. It could potentially include various methods of “ solar radiation management ”, such as brightening clouds over the oceans, or injecting reflective aerosols into the stratosphere. If any of these “climate cooling” technologies could help bring temperatures down, they need much more carefully governed research.

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is not the same as carbon capture and storage (CCS), which refers to the capture of emissions from industrial plants before they reach the atmosphere. In all net zero scenarios CCS is needed to deal with the residual emissions of fossil fuels. But we now know CDR is going to be required as well – first alongside emissions reduction, to slow warming down, and then to return the global temperature to a safer level.

There are various potential removal methods . Some are familiar and uncontroversial, though not yet being done at anything like the required scale. These are natural processes such as tree-planting, restoring ecosystems and improving carbon in soils.

Other “novel” forms of CDR are still in development. Carbon uptake methods in the oceans include enhancing the ocean’s alkalinity and the fertilisation of phytoplankton by adding iron. On land, enhanced natural processes include adding charcoal to soils (“ biochar ”), and accelerating the creation of carbonates from rock weathering .

There are also more technological interventions. These include “bioenergy with carbon capture and storage” ( Beccs ), in which biomass is burned for energy and the emissions captured and stored underground; and “direct air capture” , the removal of CO₂ from the air with advanced machines.

All of these methods are now being piloted, but remain expensive. Some of them also raise environmental risks: before any could be used at significant scale, countries would need to be sure that they would not have negative side-effects. In turn that means the world needs to think seriously about their governance.

The politics of cooling the planet

But there is currently no place for such talks. Neither novel methods of carbon dioxide removal, nor increasing the earth’s reflectivity, are formally part of the Cop negotiations or indeed any other UN policy process.

This is because many countries have believed that any discussion of these would take the pressure off emissions reduction. They have been supported in this view by some of the larger climate NGOs , who have not wanted anything to distract from their campaign against fossil fuels.

But the world has changed. Climate science says emissions reduction on its own can no longer keep us on a safe climate pathway. This surely makes blanket opposition to novel CDR and cooling methods untenable. Governments need to be scaling up research into these methods and considering their governance. At the very least, they should be talking about them.

This is why the latest moves at Cop31 are so important. At this point it is not clear whether countries will agree to a statement on how to respond to overshoot. Some are still opposed. But if the final text does acknowledge that active cooling will be needed, it will mark the beginning of a new era in climate action.

stories.body:
Unfit to Teach

Co-published with KQED

Reporting Highlights

Licensed Until Charged: Three educators who were reported to the state for alleged misconduct were allowed to keep working — and to draw new complaints — until they were criminally charged.

Incomplete Investigation: One was reported for allegedly touching children inappropriately in 2019. California didn’t suspend his credentials until his 2024 arrest.

Lack of Guidelines: California’s educator licensing agency provides no guidelines to the volunteers who review teacher misconduct cases for determining when and how to mete out punishment.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

Five years before police arrested former elementary school counselor David Braff for allegedly sexually abusing students, complaints had already been sent to the state of California: that Braff had sat students on his lap, rubbed their legs and touched them near their vaginas.

But California’s educator licensing agency failed to conduct a thorough investigation after his school district reported Braff to the state in 2019. And the agency allowed Braff to continue working with children. It wasn’t until his 2024 arrest that the agency suspended his credentials. By then, he’d gotten jobs at three more Southern California schools. At one of them, prosecutors allege, another student complained the guidance counselor had touched him, too.

The state Commission on Teacher Credentialing also delayed revoking the credentials of two other teachers who were later convicted of sexually abusing students. As with Braff, schools had reported those educators to the agency that determines who can work in California’s public schools. And as with Braff, the commission allowed those teachers to keep teaching — and draw new complaints — until after they were criminally charged, an investigation by KQED and ProPublica found. That includes a middle school math teacher who sent his student a video showing a boy’s genitals and an elementary teacher who touched students’ butts and vaginal areas and placed their hands on his crotch, according to court records.

In each of the cases, state investigators did not interview some of the students who had alleged abuse, according to the students, parents and attorneys who spoke to KQED and ProPublica. Several former agency staffers, including investigators, told the news outlets that, at times, the volunteer panel tasked with assessing teacher accusations overlooked evidence of wrongdoing. That perspective from staff members was backed up by two former members of the panel and two people who served on the state commission that ultimately decides teacher discipline.

After police arrested Braff in 2024, a parent emailed Jeffrey Weinstein, superintendent at Santa Paula Unified School District, where Braff was first accused of sexually abusing students. “Who dropped the ball and allowed this monster to still be around kids?” the parent wrote, according to public records obtained by the news outlets. (Weinstein was not working at Santa Paula at the time students accused Braff.)

In his emailed response, Weinstein blamed the state’s teacher licensing agency. He told the parent that the district had conducted its own investigation and reported the guidance counselor to the state as well as to police. He also said he had reviewed the district’s investigative file and “vehemently disagreed” with the agency’s decision not to revoke Braff’s credentials.

“We sent all the evidence we had gathered,” Weinstein said. “The district did everything in its legal capacity it could.”

Braff is soon to stand trial for sexually abusing 15 students, including 13 from Santa Paula. He has been in jail since November 2024. He has pleaded not guilty and did not respond to a request for comment sent through the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office’s electronic messaging system. His attorney declined to comment.

Braff had previously told Santa Paula Unified administrators that he did not touch students near their private parts or have them sit on his lap — and that he only gave students side hugs, high-fives, fist bumps and taps on the knee, according to the district’s 2019 report to the state.

“Mr. Braff described keeping an office environment where kids can move around; and he would not be closer than arm’s length,” the report said, summarizing the district’s interview with Braff. “It was not his intent to make them afraid but rather feel that there was someone in their corner; someone to talk to.”

Anita Fitzhugh, a spokesperson for the Commission on Teacher Credentialing, said the state automatically revokes teachers’ credentials when they are convicted of sexual criminal offenses. But she wrote in a statement that “unless the applicant or educator is convicted of a mandatory criminal offense, there are no written criteria that set the level of adverse action for educator discipline matters.” She did not answer questions about specific cases or details of the investigative process.

Fitzhugh said the state does not provide any guidelines for those reviewing teacher misconduct cases about when discipline is warranted or the type of punishment that should be meted out. And she said it was the commission’s role to balance “protecting students as well as the legal rights of educators who have been accused but not convicted.”

California’s system of disciplining educators dates to the 1970s, Fitzhugh said, and “a deep and comprehensive review of the educator discipline system, prioritizing student safety in the schools, is in order.”

“We expect the Commission to take this up in the near future,” she said.

Students Not Interviewed

In the summer of 2019, California’s Commission on Teacher Credentialing received a detailed report from the Santa Paula school district about Braff’s alleged misconduct at McKevett Elementary School. The state requires districts to report educators when they resign or are fired after allegations of misconduct. Braff, who had been a guidance counselor at the school for four years, had resigned in the midst of the district’s investigation into complaints by at least seven students that he had touched them inappropriately.

The district told the state agency that it had contemplated but did not initiate any discipline against Braff before accepting his resignation. The district said it appeared, based on student interviews, that Braff “had engaged in at least inappropriate conduct.” Its report to the state, submitted two months after he resigned, included a 20-page summary of the principal’s interviews with at least seven accusers and two witnesses. It also included Braff’s defense and noted multiple inconsistencies in his account of what had occurred.

One fifth grade girl said that during a visit to his office, Braff had locked the door, grabbed her by her hips and forced her to sit on his lap, according to the district’s report to the state of its investigation. She said she did not like being touched and cried every time she had to see him for counseling. The girl requested to transfer to another school, district investigators said, because she wanted to “be away from” Braff.

Two other girls alleged Braff touched them near their “privates,” the district reported to the state. Neither girl was aware of the other’s claim.

One of them, a fourth grader, told the principal that she had been meeting regularly with Braff for counseling since second grade. During those visits, he would make her sit on his lap. She told the principal that Braff tapped her on the leg with his hand “in a way to try to make her feel like she was doing a good job,” but she said the tapping hurt. After two school years of regular counseling, she alleged he started tapping her higher on the thigh, close to her “private.” In contrast, she said a different teacher pats students on the head when they do a good job, according to the district’s report to the state.

The girl, who is now 18, spoke to KQED and ProPublica with her mother and attorney present on the condition that only her first initial, J., be used to protect her privacy. J. said Braff had told her that whatever happened in his office was a secret. She said she had few friends at the school and was terrified of getting in trouble when she reported the person she confided in.

The district’s report to the state included notes from an interview with J.’s former principal, Lydia Olivo, who had left the school before J. and other students complained about Braff. Olivo told Santa Paula investigators that J. was “not always honest,” the report said. Olivo described Braff as a reliable employee who had strong relationships with parents, staff and students. She “seemed surprised that any of this could have occurred while she had been Principal at McKevett,” the district’s report said. Olivo did not respond to calls, emails and texts seeking comment.

During the district’s investigation, Braff acknowledged touching students on the knee. “He explained if someone is crying, he taps on the knee to say they are doing a good job to get the sad feelings out,” according to the district’s report to the state. “When asked to demonstrate, Mr. Braff showed a slap on his own knee.”

Nonetheless, the educator licensing agency appears not to have attempted to reconcile the very different accounts of Braff’s behavior. Informed of Olivo’s characterization of her complaint, J. and her mother told KQED and ProPublica that no one at the state agency had called to ask them about it or sought to verify any details, even though the district’s report to the state included J.’s contact information along with that of the other students.

“If a little girl comes up to you and says something, maybe you should not say that they’re a liar,” J. said.

“They should interview students themselves and not just rely on the school district. Do a legit investigation,” said J.’s mother, who did not know that the state had decided not to discipline Braff until the news outlets alerted her.

Fitzhugh, the spokesperson for the teacher credentialing agency, did not answer questions as to why J. was not interviewed or whether anyone else was. The case was assigned to a staffer whose job description did not include interviewing victims.

At least one other student who had reported Braff for touching her inappropriately also told KQED and ProPublica that no one from the state contacted her about her allegations.

A former agency investigator, who reviewed the district’s report to the state at the request of the news outlets, said she believed the students’ accusations because the district’s investigation described multiple children making similar claims. She also noted the contradictions in Braff’s responses. Cases involving allegations of inappropriately touching students should always be assigned to investigators trained to interview victims, she said.

“Any claim of sexual misconduct should go to somebody who’s going to be making phone calls,” said the investigator, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect her current job. “This man is grooming these children. There’s no other way to look at it to me. Their stories are credible.”

Per state law, the agency staff assigned to look into Braff’s case did not make recommendations about whether or how to discipline him. That recommendation is left up to a little-known group of volunteers who meet monthly at the agency’s Sacramento headquarters to weigh reports from state investigators, school districts, police and others. That volunteer panel sends its recommendations to the 19 commissioners of the credentialing body, most of whom are appointed by the governor.

If the panel does recommend discipline, the commissioners have the final say. However, if the panel decides that no punishment is warranted, the commissioners do not review that case.

Two former investigators at the state agency told the news organizations that the panel’s recommendations did not always align with the evidence they found. “Sometimes, as investigators, we’ll see the recommendations, and we’ll be like, ‘What the hell happened here?’” one former investigator said.

“I Was Consistently Shocked”

Over three days in December 2020, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, members of the volunteer panel, known as the Committee of Credentials, dialed into their monthly phone meeting to address 198 cases of educators accused of misconduct. Among them was Braff, who by then was working in another school.

The volunteers included a retired law enforcement officer, a school board member, a school administrator, an education consultant and several teachers. They had been selected by the commissioners for two-year terms.

State regulations give the volunteer committee broad latitude when assessing allegations of teacher misconduct and recommending discipline to the commission. Unlike jurors in a criminal trial, who need to believe a case is proven beyond a reasonable doubt in order to convict, the committee only needs to find “probable cause” before recommending a reprimand, a far lower standard.

“It’s where a normal and reasonable person would feel that there’s a chance that this person did this,” said Steve Thorpe, the former law enforcement officer who served on the committee when Braff’s case was reviewed. “It’s a low threshold. You know it when you see it.” He declined to comment on Braff’s case.

The fact that Braff’s case was not forwarded to the commissioners, former committee members said, meant the majority of the seven-member panel did not see enough evidence in the district’s investigation and the state’s report to discipline Braff.

One former committee member, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of repercussions from the teacher licensing agency, said she tends to scrutinize district investigations because administrators can misrepresent the facts or ask children leading questions.

Another former committee member who served during the Braff case said that they were generally alarmed to hear some fellow members dismiss children as unreliable sources. The person, who declined to comment on Braff’s case, spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared professional repercussions.

“I was consistently shocked,” they said. “To have committee members discuss serious allegations as, ‘Well, you know how girls can be. They say all kinds of things they don’t mean,’ is an unacceptable, antiquated point of view. What if we get this wrong? Who are we allowing in the classroom?”

By the time the committee decided against recommending punishment for Braff, he had already been working as a counselor at a different elementary school in Los Angeles for more than a year. (A former student at that charter school would tell police after Braff’s 2024 arrest that the counselor had touched the boy’s thigh near his groin when the two met in his office, according to a court transcript from his criminal case.)

In 2022, nearly two years after the state closed Braff’s case, a school administrator reported to the district that one of the girls who had accused Braff of abuse continued to suffer severe anxiety and could not be in rooms alone with men. Another had attempted suicide multiple times and spent a year in residential treatment, she wrote in an email obtained by KQED and ProPublica.

In his response, an assistant superintendent informed the administrator that the district had previously filed with the state to have Braff’s credential revoked or suspended but the agency chose not to do so. “At this point, I think pursing this matter legally is the best way to address these issues,” he wrote, referring to following up with Santa Paula police.

Santa Paula administrators did not respond to requests for comment.

Two Additional Cases

KQED and ProPublica identified at least two other educators who, like Braff, were reported by their school districts to the state for sexual misconduct but were allowed to keep teaching until they were criminally charged. Each would draw additional allegations of sexual abuse.

As in the Braff case, the volunteer committee in these two cases evaluated much of the same evidence as police, including complaints detailing students’ experiences. And in both cases, investigators with the teacher credentialing agency did not interview some victims.

In one, a Southern California school district shared with the state agency screenshots of messages that middle school math teacher Brashawn Washington had sent to his 11-year-old student, who he regularly contacted through the video game Fortnite. Those messages included a TikTok video showing another boy’s penis. (At his trial, Washington told jurors that he did not send the video to his student.)

The Romoland School District also shared with the state screenshots of Washington’s Google Hangouts chats asking the student if he worked out, calling him “guapo,” or handsome, and sending him kissing emojis.

The boy’s mother had provided the screenshots from her son’s phone to the school in May 2020, according to public records obtained from Romoland. The school district promptly alerted police and began its own investigation, filing a report to the teacher credentialing agency that summer, district records show.

The district included in its report the mother’s contact information, records show. But neither the student nor his mother were interviewed, the mother told KQED and ProPublica. Fitzhugh, the credentialing agency spokesperson, did not answer questions about how state investigators decided who, if anyone, to interview.

A Romoland administrator who said the district shared the screenshots with the state as part of its report did not answer questions about the state’s response.

Washington resigned during the school’s investigation and soon got hired at Pasadena High School starting in the fall of 2020. Washington, teaching virtually at first during the pandemic, continued messaging students over Fortnite despite district policy prohibiting personal contact with students. He had been teaching there for seven months when the volunteer committee recommended a 21-day suspension in March. (Commissioners did not approve the suspension until after school let out.)

State law did not require Washington to notify the Pasadena school district of the recommended suspension. Nor did the teacher licensing agency have to alert his new employer of any discipline if it did not know where he was employed.

Just as his suspension was set to begin in July 2021, Washington was arrested — and the state suspended his credentials indefinitely.

The next year, while out on bail, Washington sent a Pasadena High student images of himself having oral sex with another man, among other messages, according to court records. At Washington’s 2024 criminal trial, that student testified that the teacher had also asked him to share naked pictures of himself when he was 16. Washington told jurors that he did not know the student was a minor. He was sentenced to eight years and eight months in prison for multiple sex offenses , including “annoying or molesting” the Romoland student by sending him the video, as well as producing and possessing child sex abuse material related to minors who were not his students.

A spokesperson for Pasadena Unified did not respond to questions regarding Washington’s hiring or the state’s recommended discipline, but said in a written statement that the district conducts background checks during the hiring process.

Both Washington and his former attorney declined to comment.

A similar pattern unfolded with a San Francisco Bay Area elementary teacher, Matthew Shelton, who was convicted of sexually abusing four students last month.

Shelton had first been arrested in 2007 on charges of sexually abusing students in Napa Valley . Three third-graders had told police he touched their butts or crotches, or made them touch his penis during class.

Shelton was acquitted in that case, but the state’s licensing body did investigate the claims. At the time, Shelton told state investigators that the students had made up the allegations and that he passed a polygraph test, which he had obtained himself. Two of those former students told KQED and ProPublica that state investigators never interviewed them. The agency did not respond to questions about why the students were not interviewed.

In 2008, the licensing agency issued Shelton a confidential written warning, which was expunged after three years, according to trial testimony. That decision meant Shelton was able to keep teaching for the long term; he had already begun a new job in nearby Benicia.

Years later, in 2022, students began accusing Shelton of touching them inappropriately. The Benicia school district and a student’s parents reported him to the state commission in 2023. More students came forward and told police that Shelton had touched their crotch or butt over their clothing; one student said he made her touch his penis when she was in first grade during a school field trip.

Shelton resigned but quickly got a job at another school. As with the other cases, the new school said it had no information about the ongoing investigation. It also had no knowledge of his earlier warning, which had been expunged more than a decade earlier.

This time around, however, things unfolded differently: While the state did not alert the new school about any problems, a parent did. In September, just weeks into the school year, Shelton’s new employer learned from a Benicia parent about the active police investigation as well as the earlier issues in Napa.

Shelton was immediately put on leave. In February 2024, prosecutors charged him, requiring the state licensing agency to automatically suspend his credentials. Unlike in Napa, the agency revoked his license in July 2024 without waiting for a conviction.

Shelton did not respond to requests for comment, and his attorney declined to comment. He is due to be sentenced in December. Benicia Superintendent Chris Calabrese declined to comment on Shelton’s hiring.

There are significant repercussions when the state fails to take disciplinary action. For one thing, it means that other schools receive no indication of a problem. A red flag typically appears next to an educator’s name in a public database when they are punished by the Commission on Teacher Credentialing. But no such warning appears when a teacher is fired or forced to resign without state discipline, leaving their potential future employers in the dark. Nor would a confidential warning letter like the one Shelton received result in a red flag. California lawmakers have tried to address the gap, but their efforts failed .

Student victims, too, suffer long-lasting damage.

One of the students who accused Shelton in Napa told KQED and ProPublica that for years she wished she hadn’t reported him to anyone because she and her classmates were characterized as liars after “we poured out so much.”

“It could’ve been stopped with us, but it wasn’t,” she said. “They didn’t believe us.”

In Braff’s case, the Santa Paula Unified students who had accused him of abuse continued to struggle in school as their former counselor kept getting new jobs in education.

J. told KQED and ProPublica that for years she avoided acknowledging what Braff did to her. “I couldn’t place where all these emotions were coming from. I was blaming everything else except the actual problem,” J. said, referring to the abuse by Braff. “I didn’t want to live anymore.”

J., now a high school senior, has been homeschooled by her mother for almost three years. She said she still has nightmares in which Braff yells at her for “telling on him.”

And she has long faced doubts from others about her account of what happened to her in elementary school. A few years ago, she recalled, a former classmate told her: “Why would they let him go work somewhere else if he did that to you?”

stories.body:
The deal with people and a company connected to Trump was made without IRS agreement, alarming agency officials. One law professor said the deal doesn’t pass “the smell test.”

Top Trump administration officials intervened to help a longtime golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley secure a half-million-dollar payout from the IRS. A company connected to Trump’s media business also got a half-million.

The deal grew out of a little-noticed federal class-action lawsuit filed in 2025 by five individuals and companies. The group got $2.5 million after accusing the IRS of failing to protect their tax information.

The law permits a $1,000 payment to victims for each instance of an unauthorized inspection or disclosure of tax data. In this case, however, the government’s monetary settlement is 250 times higher than what the law calls for given the allegations. Victims can receive more money if they show actual damages, but multiple officials say such cases almost never result in payments approaching this size. These generous settlements have raised concerns because IRS Office of Chief Counsel attorneys were not consulted about the settlement terms, as is standard practice, according to people familiar with the case and documents seen by ProPublica.

What’s more, those payouts didn’t resolve the lawsuit. After the settlement was made, two more people came forward seeking to continue the litigation — and both are connected to Trump businesses. One is a retired accountant who worked at the same Trump property as the golf pro. The second appears to be a former lifeguard at a different Trump golf club in Westchester County, New York.

Gil Rothenberg, a law professor at American University who ran the appellate section at the Justice Department tax division for 15 years before leaving in 2019, said the deal “is not passing the smell test.”

“It’s not just the amount that I find odd and unusual,” he told ProPublica. “It’s the fact that this settlement amount occurred before any final decision by the district court, and basically the DOJ is giving up any right to appeal.”

The case in question is Safe Harbor International LLC v. Booz Allen Hamilton, Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Department of the Treasury, brought in Maryland federal court. Plaintiffs claim that the IRS and the government contractor Booz Allen failed to implement proper safeguards and were negligent in allowing Booz Allen employee Charles Littlejohn to steal tax records and give them to news organizations, including ProPublica.

President Donald Trump sued over similar claims earlier this year, seeking $10 billion in damages. In response, then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced a $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization fund” to resolve the case. That settlement was structured to grant the president’s inner circle the authority to green-light payouts of government money to whomever they wanted. The public erupted in outrage. Democratic and even a small number of Republican lawmakers objected to the proposed fund, and the department dropped the idea as Blanche sought Senate confirmation for his position.

Critics fear that the DOJ’s unusual payment in the Safe Harbor case could be a backdoor way to revive something similar to the controversial slush fund. In all, plaintiffs claim the size of the class is “in the tens or hundreds of thousands.” If a significant number of those plaintiffs secured the same payment, the total liability for the federal government could reach into the billions of dollars. A judge has yet to rule on whether to allow the case to proceed.

That group could include other Trump allies and friends. It even “opens the door to Trump himself benefiting from this settlement,” said John Koskinen, who served as IRS commissioner from 2013 to 2017.

Spokespeople for the Justice Department and IRS said they would not comment on a pending case. A White House spokesperson said that the Justice Department is “promoting efficient resolution of cases to avoid extraordinary liability.”

Between 2018 and 2020, Littlejohn, the Booz Allen contractor, leaked confidential IRS data to ProPublica and The New York Times, he has said. The data included years of Trump’s taxes and information on thousands of the wealthiest people in the country.

Do You Have a Justice Department Tip for ProPublica?

If you know about this case and the government’s handling of it, please contact our reporting team. I’m grateful for any documents that sources can share. Protecting sources is something I take very seriously.

Avi Asher-Schapiro

If you have tips about Big Tech and the Trump administration, please get in touch.

ProPublica published stories on the tax-avoidance strategies of the ultrawealthy. The New York Times reported in 2020 on how Trump declared large annual losses to avoid paying taxes. Together, the two news organizations reported that Trump was fighting with the IRS over a long-running audit that could have cost him $100 million .

Littlejohn pleaded guilty in October 2023 to unauthorized disclosure of tax information. A judge sentenced him to five years in prison .

The IRS sent letters to more than 400,000 individuals and businesses to alert them that their taxpayer information had been “inappropriately disclosed” by Littlejohn. As ProPublica has previously stated, we obtained the tax return information of the top 0.001% of individuals by income, a figure in the thousands. Limited information about other entities appears in the records only to the extent that it is related to the group of top earners.

A number of taxpayers who received the notice filed civil lawsuits demanding compensation from the IRS and Booz Allen.

The Safe Harbor class-action initially brought together five such plaintiffs who, at first glance, had nothing in common apart from having received an IRS notice about the leak.

Safe Harbor International is an obscure LLC incorporated in Delaware. It has no website or public presence and was most recently registered to a residential home in Washington, D.C. When ProPublica knocked on the door, the person living there said they’d never heard of the company.

Safe Harbor’s investors include Donald Wilson , who leads a Chicago-based financial trading firm. Last March, the Securities and Exchange Commission dropped a case brought during the Biden administration against a crypto company that Wilson controlled. A few months later, Wilson’s firm said it had invested $100 million in the president’s publicly traded media company, Trump Media and Technology Group, the owner of Truth Social.

A spokesperson for Wilson said he is a passive shareholder in Safe Harbor and “was unaware of this lawsuit until last week and has had no involvement in the litigation or any settlement discussions.” The spokesperson added that there was no connection between Wilson’s Trump Media investment and the SEC’s dismissal. “There was no quid pro quo, and the investment was not made in exchange for any regulatory action,” the spokesperson said.

The other four plaintiffs who ultimately joined Safe Harbor’s suit were Texas-based Alarm Concepts, a Connecticut company called Belpointe Sleepovation Investment, an individual in Texas named Cedrick Williams, and Shelby Lowman, the golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley.

It’s unclear if Trump knows Lowman personally. After Trump bought his Hudson Valley golf club in 2009, the Poughkeepsie Journal reported that he visited nearly every month to oversee renovations. Lowman was already working there as a golf pro and has remained at the club for the past 17 years, according to his LinkedIn profile.

In addition to his work as a golf pro, Lowman paints pastoral scenes of Trump’s golf properties. Trump has autographed copies of Lowman’s paintings to be given out as prizes for golf competitions at the club. The golf club has also posted a photo of Lowman posing with Eric Trump, who runs the Trump Organization.

A spokesperson for the Trump Organization said it “had no involvement in or connection to this lawsuit. To the extent any current or former employees are involved, it is entirely in their personal capacity as individual taxpayers.”

At first, the Justice Department sought to dismiss the Safe Harbor case . A DOJ trial attorney argued, among other things, that the U.S. government was not the proper target for a lawsuit about the conduct of a government contractor. The judge rejected the motion and cleared the way for discovery and potentially a trial.

The plaintiffs in Safe Harbor alleged two unauthorized disclosures of their tax information, which would entitle them to $2,000 each under the statute. To get more, they would have to prove actual damages. But before the case reached the fact-finding stage, the DOJ stopped fighting the case and in August made a unilateral proposal to the five named plaintiffs, labeled an offer of judgment, to resolve the matter by paying them $500,000 each, court records show.

When IRS employees learned about the DOJ’s $2.5 million offer, they pointed out that it was dramatically higher than what the law called for and was not supported by any evidence, according to people familiar with the case and documents seen by ProPublica.

What made the government’s offer even more unusual was who made it. The career DOJ trial attorney working the case did not sign the proposed payout, as is typical.

Instead, two Trump political appointees delivered the offer : Brett Shumate, the head of the DOJ’s civil division, and Joshua Wu, the deputy assistant attorney general for the department’s tax litigation branch. (Shumate left the DOJ in early November. He did not respond to requests for comment.)

In the past, the IRS has fought such claims. In 2022, billionaire investor Ken Griffin brought a similar suit against the agency, dropping it a year and a half later after he received an apology from the IRS and a pledge to improve the agency’s data security. Griffin received no money as part of the settlement.

Lowman, Williams and Alarm Concepts did not respond to requests for comment. Reached by phone, Linda Nussbaum, a lawyer for Belpointe, told ProPublica that it was “news to me” that the other plaintiffs in the lawsuit had “ties to the Trump administration.” She declined to comment further on the case.

stories.title: The Seduction of Donald Trump
stories.summary: Trump's quest to make his mark on the global stage threatens to be catastrophic. But it could be worse. The post The Seduction of Donald Trump appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and China's President Xi Jinping greet each other before the welcome banquet for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026 in Shenzhen, China (Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)

It was truly galling when Richard Nixon, the disgraced former U.S. president, became a respected elder statesman late in life. He published an embarrassment of a book on U.S.-Soviet relations in 1980—that nonetheless influenced incoming president Ronald Reagan. He traveled to Beijing after the Tiananmen Square massacre of 1989 in order to revive U.S.-Chinese relations by emphasizing commerce over morality. He had the ear of presidents from Ford to Clinton, which buoyed his reputation for geopolitical acuity even if what he had to say was just regurgitated realism.

Donald Trump has suffered a lifetime of disgraces—multiple bankruptcies, a gazillion lawsuits, a felony conviction, two impeachments, an election loss in 2020, and, earlier this month, a midterm repudiation. The cumulative effect of these public failures would prompt ordinary people to change their names, endure cosmetic surgery, and relocate to an obscure corner of the globe.

But shameless politicos, like Nixon and Trump, are always looking to regain the spotlight. Unlike Nixon, Trump did not try to resurrect his reputation as a post-presidential hobby. Instead he regained the Oval Office in 2024 largely to prove that he was right all along, despite all these setbacks. Over the last two years, he hasn’t made his case for redemption through arguments or by setting positive examples. Instead, he has focused on lying, bullying, and going after his enemies.

The next two years will include all of that, of course, but Trump is also likely to take a page from Nixon’s book by making his mark on international affairs. By this I don’t mean a fling with a Slovenian supermodel, though this is basically the sum total of Trump’s pre-presidential experience with foreign policy.

Trump has wanted to acquire the title of “elder statesman” ever since he returned to the Oval Office. Bagging a Nobel Peace Prize would have been an effective shortcut to this goal. To bolster his case for the prize, he has made bold claims about ending wars and heading off conflicts. By punishing bad guys—Maduro, Khamenei—he effectively styles himself as the ultimate good guy. The superpowers that he deploys—the Massive Ordnance Air Blast, the tariff, the sanction, the insult—all support his boast that he is righting historic wrongs.

In his final two years in office, Trump won’t be able to do much on the home front, thanks to a confrontational Congress. Instead, he will try to burnish—at least in his own mind—his foreign policy credentials. He will do so not through the conventional route of promoting democracy or making grand humanitarian gestures. Rather, he will stay within his comfort zone by focusing on making backroom deals with fellow strongmen.

The first stop on his two-year swan song of a world tour will be this week in Shenzhen, China.

The Troika

Once again channeling Nixon, Donald Trump wants to do something big on nuclear weapons. For Nixon, arms control negotiations were an opportunity to manage risk with the Soviet Union and, through the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, preserve the hegemonic power of the nuclear club, primarily the United States.

Trump, by contrast, doesn’t seem quite sure what he thinks about nuclear weapons.

The president has insisted that the United States has fallen behind in the nuclear race and must regain its number one position. Toward that end, the Trump administration has proposed a dramatic increase in spending on nuclear weapons to $71 billion as part of the $1.5 trillion defense budget. Over 30 years, the nuclear modernization program will cost $1.7 trillion . This is money spent, of course, on deterrence. But the president has also, from time to time, hinted at the use of nuclear weapons, most recently with his threats to annihilate Iran .

At the same time, Trump has talked about the importance of reaching nuclear arms control agreements with Russia and China. “There’s no reason for us to be building brand new nuclear weapons, we already have so many,” he said back in February 2025 , shortly after taking office. “You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.”

That perhaps is the definition of world leader: someone who loudly laments all the money wasted on dangerous nuclear weapons even as they allocate even more funds to modernize the arsenal.

In any case, Trump is in China this week to cajole Putin and Xi into agreeing to something related to nuclear weapons. It’s going to be a heavy lift. Given the gap in size in the respective arsenals, China doesn’t believe that it has enough weapons to justify any limits. And Russia is in no mood to negotiate these days, despite the economic challenges it faces as a result of the war in Ukraine.

Actually, Trump has a lousy record when it comes to arms control. He tried to get trilateral discussions started in his first term but failed to extend the one major agreement with Russia, New START (which Biden ultimately secured). Then, in this term, Trump failed again to deal with a Russian proposal to limit deployment of nuclear weapons.

But nukes are not only thing on Trump’s mind.

A New Yalta?

Near the end of World War II, Franklin Delano Roosevelt met with Stalin and Winston Churchill at Yalta to discuss the post-war order. On the agenda was the future of Germany and Japan, the borders in and around Eastern Europe, the question of reparations, and the shape and functions of the United Nations.

Such a meeting of winners surely appeals to Trump, who wants only to sit at the big boy’s table since everything else is too low stakes for a superhero like himself. So, for instance, Trump arrived at this week’s meeting of Southeast Asian leaders so late that he could do little more than pose in the group photo. He has no interest in the United Nations, which he views solely as a once-a-year opportunity to hector the international community. He has experimented with his Board of Peace, which has barely had any effect in Gaza much less address other global problems.

Trump has put more emphasis on face-to-face meetings with Putin and Xi, though such bilateral negotiations have not yielded much either. He met Putin in Alaska last year and has conducted three sessions with Xi. The meeting with the Russian leader was all pomp and no circumstance. A few deals were concluded with Xi but nothing groundbreaking.

But a president can still dream. And Trump imagines that in Shenzhen he can put his name on a new security order in Europe, a superpower agreement on non-proliferation, perhaps even a roadmap for peace in the Middle East. All that’s required is a bit of autocrat-wrangling, which Trump prides himself on being an expert.

But the only person likely to be wrangled in Shenzhen is Trump himself. He has revealed a keen ability to be snowed by Putin, who has nimbly avoided additional sanctions and won various favors from the Trump administration in exchange for…what? The Russian leader has proven worse than uncompromising in negotiations around the war in Ukraine, most recently in Abu Dhabi where he insisted that NATO return to its pre-1997 deployments .

Instead of offering to compromise on Ukraine—on territory or security guarantees or even ceasefires—Putin is offering Trump something much dearer to the U.S. president’s heart: access to Russian fossil fuel riches.

According to The New York Times , Russia has been offering to sell off Lukoil assets—oil fields, refineries, gas stations—to a close Trump ally (Todd Boehly), two Gulf investors with ties to Jared Kushner (Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat), and an Emirati royal connected to Steve Witkoff (Sheikh Tahnoon). The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation would also get a piece of the action. Corruption, which was a top issue in the U.S. midterm elections , continues to be a guiding principle of policymaking in the Trump administration.

China has seduced Trump in a different way. It fell back on a more traditional honeypot scheme to ensnare Trump’s key computer chip ally, Jensen Huang of Nvidia. It just so happens that Nvidia is the only company that produces the chips necessary for the most powerful AI applications. And it just so happens that Huang, who was having an affair with a reputed Chinese spy, was lobbying Trump to send more of those chips to China.

Such traditional spycraft aside, China has been content to stand back and benefit from Trump’s self-inflicted wounds—the disastrous war with Iran, the tariffs against allies and adversaries, and the withdrawal from international agreements and institutions. Perhaps Trump is only accelerating U.S. decline, but China is grateful nonetheless for the revised timeline.

Putin wants to play Trump. China is happy to let Trump be Trump. They both relish the opportunity in Shenzhen to feed Trump’s delusions of grandeur. They’ll give the U.S. president a stage on which he can strut as an elder statesman. They’ll give him compliments.

But they won’t give him any real agreements.

The Next Two Years

Nixon was loathsome, to be sure, but he wasn’t stupid. Tutored by Henry Kissinger, the former president at least understood the basics of geopolitics. Also, his attempt to launder his reputation was basically harmless, at least compared to the war crimes he committed as president.

Trump, on the other hand, can do immense damage in his last two years in office. Blocked by Congress from doing more DOGE-like damage to the U.S. government, he will turn his attention to furthering his campaign to destroy international institutions. The war the administration has launched against the International Criminal Court will serve as a model.

The seduction of Trump by Putin and Xi—along with lesser autocrats like Modi, Erdogan, and Milei—could have even more damaging consequences. Putin will wield Trump like a machete to cut the strings that hold together NATO and the European Union. China will use Trump’s anti-internationalism to remake global affairs in its own image—mercantile, extractivist, autocratic. Trump, seduced, will think that he is at the helm, an elder statesman coming into his own, putting his mark on the world much as he is making his mark on Washington, DC.

With Trump, this might be the best-case scenario. The alternative—increased conflict with Russia or China or both—would be even more catastrophic. Yes, it’s a horrifying prospect, but let Trump believe that he is remaking the world.

It’s better than his unmaking of it.

stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .

stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature. Mei’s case was hailed by Chinese media as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain.
