stories.title: Venezuela’s Base Deal Has No Voters
stories.summary: Venezuelans deserve democracy before, not after, a military deal with the United States. The post Venezuela’s Base Deal Has No Voters appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright speaks with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez during a press conference regarding the oil agreement reached by the US government and Venezuela on September 2, 2026 in Caracas, Venezuela. (Jesus Vargas/Getty Images)

In his first week as Venezuela’s foreign minister, Oliver Blanco sat down with Marco Rubio at the State Department on November 2. The official readout spoke of electoral reforms, political prisoners and the president’s three-phase plan : stabilization first, then economic recovery and reconciliation, and only then a democratic transition. It said nothing about soldiers.

A day later, The New York Times reported that the State Department, under Rubio, is negotiating a status of forces agreement with Caracas that would lay the foundation for a long-term American military presence. Troop numbers and locations would be settled in later agreements.

Washington will sell this as paperwork. The State Department says it has negotiated such pacts with more than 100 countries, which give American forces a predictable legal footing for ship visits, training, and exercises. Seen from outside Washington, Venezuela is not merely the latest entry on that list. It is a country whose president was seized by American troops on January 3 , whose interim leader holds no electoral mandate, and whose oil now carries a Pentagon stake.

A status of forces agreement signed under those conditions does not regulate a relationship between two sovereign governments. It writes a protectorate into law before the protected get a vote.

The soldiers, in fact, are arriving ahead of the lawyers. On October 30, Venezuelan drones and helicopters struck a Colombian National Liberation Army (ELN) camp in Apure state near the border with Colombia, and four U.S. officials told The Times that Washington supplied intelligence and drone support. The border rights group FundaRedes counted 23 victim s . Back in June, a Southern Command airstrike killed Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, a founder of Tren de Aragua, with CIA intelligence and Venezuelan forces taking part. After the June earthquakes, about 2,000 American troops moved into and around the country before pulling out again. The reopened U.S. embassy in Caracas already has a military attaché.

The readout leaves out an important motive for a future military base: the oil fields. In September, the administration announced a deal giving Washington a stake in about one-fifth of Venezuela’s oil resources. Caracas handed North American Blue Energy Partners, the vehicle of oilman Alejandro Betancourt, 100-year rights over 17 oilfields holding 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. The Pentagon owns 35 percent of that company, and Washington is guaranteed the right to buy a fifth of its output at cost.

Nobody leaves a century-long concession, part-owned by the Defense Department, without a guard. Donald Trump , speaking in Washington the same Monday Blanco visited, did not bother with euphemism. He referred to “our conquest of Venezuela.” Oil contracts are written for decades. So, it seems, are the garrisons that guard them.

Latin America has lived through this imbroglio before. In 1901, Cuba had to accept the Platt Amendment before American forces would leave, and the State Department’s historians list among its conditions the sale or lease of land for naval stations. The Guantánamo lease followed in February 1903. Washington repealed the amendment in 1934 and kept the lease, and the naval base still operates. The political tutelage was renegotiated. The military footprint signed during the tutelage outlived everyone who signed it.

The interim authority across the table from Rubio is in no position to bargain hard, and it has no mandate to bargain at all. Delcy Rodríguez has given no election date. Trump says Venezuela is not ready for elections. María Corina Machado, back after ten months in exile, wants a presidential vote by July. On Monday, teachers, nurses and university unions held a 12-hour national stoppage , demanding a $960 year-end payment that the government had left unanswered . The minimum monthly income stands at $240 . A government that cannot settle with its teachers is settling the legal status of foreign soldiers. Venezuelans can read that order of priorities. So can every capital in the hemisphere.

The counterargument deserves a fair hearing. Status of forces agreements are mundane instruments, and most of them govern exercises rather than occupations. The ELN and Tren de Aragua are real, and a Venezuelan army that sheltered guerrillas for years is now bombing them. The State Department insists that no base talks are under way.

But that is exactly the design of the deal. The framework comes first, and everything that matters (numbers, locations, duration) would be part of follow-on arrangements that neither an elected Venezuelan legislature nor the U.S. Senate will ever vote on.

The Democratic majorities that won both chambers on November 3 have three ways to keep this interim arrangement from hardening.

First, demand the text. State Department officials briefed some congressional aides on the talks in late October. A briefing for aides is not oversight.

Second, insist on the treaty form. Basing and status arrangements are usually concluded as executive agreements, not treaties. Venezuela is the case for the exception. An open-ended military presence in a country the United States attacked 10 months ago is the kind of commitment the Constitution leaves to two-thirds of the Senate.

Third, use the purse. A rider barring funds for any permanent presence in Venezuela until an elected government ratifies the arrangement would cost Washington nothing it needs this year. It would cost the oil concession its armed guarantee, and for obvious reasons the White House will fight it.

The timing gives the game away. If Rubio signs the agreement before the new Congress convenes in January, an outgoing majority and an unelected partner will have settled the matter between them, and Venezuelans will inherit the deal the way Cubans inherited Guantánamo. If the deal waits for a Senate vote and an elected government in Caracas, it may still go through. At least it will have voters behind it.

stories.title: Troubled Waters: Lake Victoria Faces an Ecological Reckoning

stories.body:
A Catholic priest offers a blessing on the shores of Lake Victoria. Priests perform rituals at landing sites, praying for bountiful catches at an increasingly unpredictable time.

PHOTO ESSAY

The largest tropical lake on Earth, Lake Victoria is under enormous strain, with its waters contaminated, fisheries decimated, and historic shorelines drowning. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, which supports more than 45 million people across the region.

By Matilde Gattoni and Matteo Fagotto • November 19, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Lake Victoria, the largest tropical lake on Earth, is under enormous strain as overfishing, pollution, and a changing climate are decimating its fisheries, contaminating its waters, and bringing record floods to its shores. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, whose basin supports more than 45 million people across the region.

For decades, Lake Victoria’s fishing industry relied on bountiful catches of Nile tilapia and Nile perch, both introduced to the lake in the 1950s. The perch, a voracious predator blamed for the disappearance of some 200 native cichlid species, became the lake’s most lucrative prize, with its filets exported to Europe and the Middle East. In recent years, overfishing has dramatically reduced fish stocks, including perch, pushing many fishermen to use illegal fine-mesh nets that catch juvenile fish before they can reproduce. Kenya’s catch fell from 94,349 metric tons in 2021 to 70,231 metric tons in 2025, according to the country’s fisheries service. In Uganda, the number of plants processing Nile perch has dropped from 21 to six, according to the director of operations at Victoria Treasures, one of the few surviving factories.

Pollution from farms, gold mining, and booming shoreline cities — including Kampala, Uganda’s capital, and Mwanza, Tanzania’s second-largest city — has compounded the damage as untreated sewage and fertilizers feed recurring algal blooms and water hyacinth invasions, which starve the water of oxygen and suffocate fish.

Yale Environment 360 / Created with Datawrapper

Making matters worse, exceptional rains linked with climate change lifted the lake to record levels in 2020 and again in 2024. The floods have forced hundreds of thousands of people from their homes and swallowed farmland and fish landing sites. The World Meteorological Organization expects this year’s El Niño, which typically brings heavier rains to East Africa, to last into 2027, raising the risk of further displacement.

In July, during the UNESCO World Heritage Committee meeting in Busan, South Korea, more than 100 civil society groups from 35 countries proposed recognizing Lake Victoria as a living cultural landscape, based on the fishing knowledge, rituals, and oral traditions its lakeside communities have accumulated over generations. The groups insisted that any nomination should protect local communities from displacement and safeguard the livelihoods of both fishers and the women who sell their catch.

If approved, inscription on the World Heritage list could bring international attention, technical help, and limited funding. It would also commit the governments of Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania to protecting the lake under an agreed management plan.

Photographer Matilde Gattoni spent February and March on Lake Victoria’s Kenyan, Ugandan, and Tanzanian shores. This photo essay combines images that reflect the lake’s dire condition — from the water hyacinths that clog landing sites to the residents displaced by floods — with images that speak to the countless ties, both economic and spiritual, that continue to bind the people to the lake.

Scroll down to see the images, or click on the photo below to launch a slideshow.

Invasive water hyacinth in Ogenya, Kenya, robs the lake of dissolved oxygen and blocks sunlight from penetrating the water. The weed, pushed by the wind into shallow areas, also keeps fishermen from reaching open water.

In Sindo, Kenya, women working as fishmongers vie for a piece of a dwindling catch. The competition has led to jaboya , or “sex for fish”: Women must trade sexual favors with fishermen to secure enough product to provide for their families.

Joyce Akinyi Odiko, 53, began as a fish seller but eventually assembled her own fleet of 30 boats, becoming one of the few women on the lake to own what she catches. As fisheries collapse in Uhania, Kenya, she is considering selling her boats and leaving fishing behind.

A trader sells omena and fried fish in the largest market in Kisumu, Kenya. Populations of omena have plummeted as a result of overfishing and warming that is reducing oxygen levels in the lake.

A young woman in Uhanya, Kenya, wades through the submerged ruins of a communal fish processing site. In many coastal villages, floods have swallowed infrastructure, displaced residents, and moved the shoreline hundreds of feet inland.

Rising lake levels destroyed the mud and log home of Jane Anyango Okelo, in Ogenya. When the water receded it left behind highly fertile soil for crops, but Jane and her husband can’t afford to rebuild their home and now live in a makeshift tent.

A girl eats her only meal of the day in an alley of the informal camp at the Kigungu landing site in Uganda. Most of the people here are refugees from Makusa and Lwamunyo islands, which were almost entirely submerged by floods in 2020.

Many fishermen have turned to sand mining in nearby river mouths as fish stocks have shrunk. The practice is illegal as dredging destroys vital fish breeding grounds, disturbs the habitats of hippos and crocodiles, and leads to the erosion of wetlands.

A laborer carries a massive bundle of rice hay on his back after the harvest in Nduru, Kenya. Fertilizer runoff from farms in the region flows directly into the nearby Nyando River and into Lake Victoria, fueling the growth of invasive water hyacinth that chokes the shoreline.

Mercury used in informal and largely unregulated gold mining operations in Macalder, Kenya, can spill into rivers that eventually discharge into Lake Victoria.

A young girl in Kigungu examines a freshly caught Nile perch. Stocks of the highly profitable fish have dwindled, so processing companies now hire agents to scour landing sites and rush large specimens to factories for export.

stories.title: A Generation Revolts
stories.summary: The post A Generation Revolts appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
We are witnessing one of the biggest generational conflicts in decades: a global revolution against a gerontocracy.

John Last is a freelance journalist and former foreign correspondent living outside Ottawa, Canada.

Across Europe, young people are being arrested in their thousands. In Milan, jackbooted soldiers from the Italian military — average age, 38 — haul protesters, some of whom are as young as 12 and 13, away from picket lines and into armored vehicles. Italy’s government — average age, 60 — has passed a new decree allowing detainments for up to 24 hours without charge. Vandals can now be arrested 48 hours after their crimes; Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, 53, has called for their parents to face financial penalties too.

Italy’s weekend of protests at the end of October, in at least a dozen major cities, was the most destructive in recent memory. In Milan, hooded youths looted the city’s luxury stores, pilfering products, one reporter wrote , “that they cannot afford and may never be able to buy.” But as shocking as Italy’s protests have been, they pale in comparison to those in France. Mobs of people have paralyzed city centers across the country for weeks. The grand streets of Paris have been blanketed in acrid smoke. French President Emmanuel Macron has accused an alliance of “radical far-left groups [and] criminals” of trying “to bring down the Republic.” Fifty-three police officers were injured over the course of a single weekend.

After more than a month, it is almost hard to believe that protests of this magnitude began over the failures of a university application portal . But by now, the grievances have multiplied: the high cost of fuel, the crowding of schools, the inaccessibility of housing, the growing precarity of work. In turn, the protests have taken on an existential desperation. An unmistakable vibe of despair permeates the masked protesters. “They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can’t say anything,” one protester in Paris told the BBC. “It’s been too long, it’s been too much.”

“They” are the elder-elite of Europe, the now-aged baby boomers who greedily gobbled up the assets of their societies: a third of Italy’s housing stock; a quarter of France’s public spending; 98% of the average Spanish worker’s salary, in the form of monthly rent. While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — they cash in. Rising prices, precarious work, broken schools: As a generation, the boomers have remained largely unaffected while the value of their real estate and investments boomed. As their wealth and number grew, they came to set the agendas of unions, politicians and the media, and they bent the state to suppress any who would rally against them. They pioneered a playbook to extract the last cents of value from Europe’s bloated and aging welfare states before departing a world they leave on the threshold of self-destruction.

But the underclass in their wake cannot be restrained forever. In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long; like the dwarves of Moria, they accidentally unleashed a primal foe. “It has been called the children’s war,” La Repubblica reports : an insurgency against calcifying Western gerontocracies waged by their own offspring.

“While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — the now-aged baby boomers cash in.”

In some ways, generational inequality is felt before it can be measured. It is usually assumed that people naturally accumulate wealth over their lifetime, and that a person in their ‘70s should own more in assets than a relatively new worker in their ‘30s. But it wasn’t always so. Today’s old-age security is the result of a general crisis of elder poverty that proliferated across the Western world in the 1920s and ‘30s when people still literally worked themselves to death, or else died penniless. To solve this problem, states embraced a system of “asymmetric socialization,” according to Pieter Vanhuysse, a leading expert in political demography at the University of Southern Denmark. In short, the state took care of the elderly while the family was still mostly expected to take care of the young.

Today, it is hard to imagine a crisis of elder poverty on a similar scale to that of the 1930s, not least because the elderly account for such a large percentage of the population. In France and Italy, thanks to longer lifespans and low rates of reproduction, the number of citizens over 65 has doubled since the arrival of the boomer generation, born between 1946 and 1964, to one in five and one in four residents, respectively. Nor is the phenomenon limited to Europe. In the United States, where fertility rates are higher, the median age has risen by 10 years since 1960. There are fewer than a billion seniors in the world today; by 2060, that number is expected to double and account for a fifth of global population.

As seniors have exploded in number, they have exercised an ever-greater influence on politics. In France, the United Kingdom, Germany, the U.S. and many other developed nations, those aged 65 and over are between 10% and 20% more likely to vote than those aged 18-25. This has contributed to a shocking representative gap — people under 30 account for half of the world’s population but just 2% of its legislators. “There’s a clear representational deficit,” said Daniel Stockemer, a political scientist at the University of Ottawa. “It creates a problem that youth’s concerns are not taken sufficiently into consideration, that youth are not sufficiently included in decision-making processes.”

In a study of intergenerational fairness in state spending, Vanhuysse found a disproportionate favoritism toward the old in nearly all the countries surveyed. Nearly a quarter of young Europeans and nearly half of young Americans are struggling financially; they will also disproportionately bear the weight of the ecological destruction and public debt accumulated by the boomers.

France, where youth first took to the streets, is among the worst offenders. There, public debt now exceeds the value of its economy. In Vanhuysse’s index, it ranks just behind Japan for the disproportionate political power it grants the elderly — nearly two in five civil servants are over 50 , a number that has rapidly increased since 2011. Vanhuysse estimates roughly $5 is spent on elderly citizens for every $1 spent on youth. That is clearly evident in the crumbling, overcrowded schools and inadequate universities that first spurred young people onto the streets. State pensions, meanwhile, eat up a quarter of the country’s public spending — including a whole third of the education ministry’s budget.

“Hopelessness is infectious, and we’re in a pandemic.”

All of this would not be so galling if it were not for the fact that the generation now draining state coffers already benefited from an unprecedented golden age of growth. Boomers entered the workforce at the peak of unionization and enjoyed stable employment, wages that beat inflation and guaranteed pensions upon retirement. They were buying starter homes when housing could be had for just two or three years’ income. Today it is nearly 10 .

Boomers used this unprecedented growth to acquire assets well beyond their needs, sitting on valuable housing stock — 28% of family homes in the U.S., for example — desperately desired by the next generation. Then they leveraged those assets to squeeze younger generations. In Australia, seniors’ investment in rental properties has increased 1,500% at the same time as rents have nearly doubled. Where boomers were able to buy property cheaply and grow their money in investments, young people today spend a vast percentage of their earnings on rent — which, more often than not, is passive income for elderly landlords.

The result is a generation that feels it has been actively held back from achieving the same or better lives than their parents had by that same generation’s relentless extraction of money. Today, Vanhuysse found, a working person in France can expect their lifetime wealth to be 17% lower than that of a baby boomer. “That’s the same difference as being, today in France, a parent of two or a parent of none,” Vanhuysse said, or “of being — hold on for this — a migrant in France or not a migrant in France.”

Far from demonstrating concern for their children, boomers have become the archetype of the hectoring elder, demanding young people live in grim austerity or else be accused of moral failing. Meanwhile, they have led the charge against any policies that would address this imbalance: cuts to pension funding, extensions of the retirement age, freezes on rent, ends to tax breaks on capital gains, the construction of new housing. They have insisted on their right to rent-seek, to economically stunt their own children’s generation. And worse, they have, where possible, actively enshrined this inequality in law.

In the last 10 years, we’ve witnessed the emergence of a two-tiered economy: one offering secure employment and benefits to senior workers and a select few entrants, and a precarious gig economy for anyone else. Nowhere is this clearer than in Italy, which deflated a staggering 42% youth unemployment rate by passing a law allowing for short-term contracts — but only for workers hired after 2014. Today, 40% of those under 29 struggle with precarious employment, compared to just 5% of those over 50. Read Noema in print.

“In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long.”

Italy’s example is particularly stark, but this phenomenon plays out, with slight variations, across the Western world. As a union steward for Canada’s public broadcaster, I witnessed it firsthand: entrenched, often incompetent or disengaged elderly employees guaranteed healthy pensions and generous leave, enabled by the labor of an army of precarious young temps who were denied benefits, moved around and kept on exploitative short-term contracts, always hoping for some vanishing chance at security. The union fought tooth and nail to protect its incumbents; new workers, meanwhile, were expected to “do the time” in employment conditions that their elders had never been asked to endure.

The advent of AI and the ongoing liberalization of the marketplace have only added fuel to this dumpster fire, eliminating entry-level positions, complicating hiring with meaningless and time-consuming tests, and generally increasing the demands of employers. Those under 40 have probably lost count of the major economic disruptions they have been expected to adapt to (I can still remember when we were all being told to learn to code ). Now, still working their way toward stable jobs, home ownership and families, they are bracing for a reality where, if AI doesn’t steal their jobs, it may well collapse the economy instead.

Amid all this chaos, young people have been largely left to fend for themselves. It’s no coincidence that the underfunding of schools prompted this outbreak of violence: Despite a staggering rise in the diagnosis of learning disabilities, classes are often crammed with more students per teacher than ever before. Ten percent of teaching hours go untaught in France because of chronic teacher absenteeism. Parents, too, have taken leave of their responsibilities. One of the possible defenses of Vanhuysse’s “asymmetric socialization” is that, while seniors benefit from wealth transfers via taxes, parents transfer wealth to their children in the form of time — the equivalent of up to seven months’ wages a year, Vanhuysse estimated . But can we really say that’s the case when Gen Z and Gen Alpha are partly defined by the countless hours they were left glued to a screen, largely unsupervised, the unfiltered internet doing untold damage to their psyches?

Elders and politicians love to blame social media for a worrying rise in youth extremism and violence. But that’s not the only cause of the dark, seething nihilism at the heart of the generations now coming of age. Stockemer calls it a “vicious cycle of political alienation”: politicians serve elderly interests, young people disengage from politics and the next government has even less motivation to address their concerns. It has reached the point that politicians openly talk about younger generations as though they are an enemy and treat them accordingly by suspending many of their rights. Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has pioneered new methods in the overpolicing of the young: banning raves, lowering the age of criminal culpability and increasing juvenile detention by 50%. A communique from the October 17 Movement, one of the organizing groups behind Italy’s protests, captures the new reality: “A government that responds to the dissatisfaction of a generation with soldiers, handcuffs and decrees does not want to listen.”

But if governments won’t listen, why won’t the boomers who elect them? How can the outpouring of despair on the streets of Europe’s capitals not be enough to move them to cede some of their wealth to the next in line?

If it feels like theirs is a generation for whom no amount of money is enough, it may be because many of them genuinely feel that way, and for good reason. A lot of them grew up believing a millionaire was a rarefied thing. But now, a million dollars is barely enough to guarantee that a 65-year-old will spend their final years in comfort. The so-called “peak boomers” turning 65 between now and 2030 can reasonably expect to live another 20 years, and medical advancements may continue to extend their lifetimes. If they stop earning and investing, they will become victims of the same economic forces they unleashed on younger generations. High housing costs are preventing many seniors from downsizing as expected, high inflation is eating into the value of benefits and the side hustles and part-time jobs that once saved seniors from penury are scarcer than ever.

Looming behind this fear is the privatized eldercare market, which has become the norm in Europe as it has long been in North America. In European countries, the average home care starts at more than $1,000 per month and only climbs from there. Residential care can cost seniors or their families tens of thousands every year. The savings that were supposed to fund the “great wealth transfer” — the mass inheritance of more than $100 trillion in assets accumulated by boomers over their lifetime — are instead being siphoned away by an oligarchy of health care companies. No wonder medically assisted suicide is becoming more popular.

The reality is that neoliberal capitalism of the kind long championed by Macron has proven to be not very good at taking care of anyone except those now at liberty to make a lot more capital. The renowned French economist Thomas Piketty pointed out that the unprecedented 20% cut in per-student funding that prompted France’s protests came at a time when, according to some measures, “France has never been richer.” At the same time as public debt has ballooned out of control, the country’s privately held wealth has doubled in proportion to the country’s GDP, “with extreme concentration among the wealthiest financial fortunes.” “The problem to solve,” he wrote, “is simply one of distribution.”

In this way, these protests are revealing all sorts of new solidarities — not only between youth struggling to pay rent and seniors fearful of the cost of care, but between the disillusioned elite of European universities and the underpaid truck drivers of Italy, or the migrant teenager from the banlieues and the middle-class couples who can’t afford a child. All are part of the growing class of losers in the economy of today — an economy fatally consumed by presentism, unable and unwilling to consider the greater, long-term good.

Gerontocracy is certainly a contributor to that problem — after all, old people have less of a stake in the future. But in reality, the petty landlord milking tenants, the civil servant counting his days to retirement and the teenager looting Decathlon have much in common: They are all dogs fighting for scraps.

“Still working their way toward stable jobs, affording homes and having families, young people are bracing for a reality where, if AI doesn’t steal their job, it may well collapse the economy instead.”

This is perhaps the thing that earlier protesters in the historic youth uprisings in Nepal and India were able to see much more clearly than their counterparts in the more affluent regions of Europe, and may indeed be behind their relative success. Hopelessness is infectious, and we’re in a pandemic. There is little to separate a trucker who cannot pay for their gas from a student who cannot pay for their rent. Both are facing a profound existential crisis for which they bear little, if any, responsibility — a crisis their governments feel duty-bound to ignore.

It is in moments like this that the extraparliamentary politics of the street flourish. In some sense, this is a return to form for the politics of Europe. “We are quite used to the idea that everything should be oriented towards consensus,” Enrico Biale, an associate professor of political philosophy at University of Piemonte Orientale, told me. “Any form of strong protest is considered a challenge that needs to be contained aggressively.” But 50 years ago, discontented students flooded the ranks of the Red Army Faction and the Brigate Rosse , which terrorized fascist sympathizers (and plenty of bystanders) across the continent. In the ‘90s, Italy’s Pantera student movement paralyzed campuses and city centers over a bill to corporatize the universities; in the 1980s, French students did much the same . Those generations were closer to the violence of a real war, but they were arguably in no way as desperate as today’s youth.

That desperation had some of the analysts I spoke to on edge. There has been a different quality to these protests than past movements for change: a toxic mix of despair and nihilism. Many of those arrested for vandalism have no prior criminal record or connections to political movements. It’s unclear what, if anything, unites them, besides a complete lack of faith in conventional authorities and their processes. “We don’t trust the institutions of this government,” the October 17 Movement communique reads , and “we don’t trust the traditional political structures [which] have been trying to profit from and monopolize struggles for decades.”

This is the fruit of the short-termism natural to gerontocracy. And it is a boon to opportunists of all kinds — the criminal, the bigot, the fascist. Generational conflict is far more universal, and more inevitable, than a race war, and it has already become a recruiting tool for haters and nihilists of every description. Whether these protests, historic though they may be, result in any meaningful change is doubtful; Stockemer, for his part, is neither impressed nor optimistic. “There’s this big outbreak of rage,” he said. “Then we wait two years, and there’s another outbreak of rage.”

But with each chime of the futile clock, Europe’s youth becomes more disillusioned, and more radicalized. Eventually, that clock will run out — and then, no pension will be generous enough to spare the elderly their discomfort.

stories.body:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.

As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

stories.body:
Sanae Takaichi cuts lonely figure at airport, a move by China that is being linked to the simmering row over Taiwan

Apec’s Chinese hosts went out of their way to give world leaders a warm welcome as they arrived in Shenzhen this week. Military bands played, dozens of cheering young men and women waved colourful bouquets, and senior officials offered hugs and handshakes on the tarmac.

But there was one exception: Japan ’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi .

The red carpet was rolled out for her arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport, but Takaichi, on her first visit to China since taking office just over a year ago, had to make do with a modest guard of honour and a welcome from a relatively junior Chinese government official.

The contrast in hospitality was impossible to ignore. Donald Trump was personally greeted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping as he stepped off Air Force One, while Vladimir Putin was met by Cai Qi, a senior Communist party official and one of Xi’s closest aides.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , beamed as he walked past rows of women in white shirts and pink skirts while soldiers from the People’s Liberation Army stood to attention, bayonets fixed. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, and the country’s first lady, Kim Hea Kyung, were given similar VIP treatment.

Takaichi, on the other hand, was met off her plane by Zhang Qiyue, China’s former ambassador to Greece, a position below those who greeted other leaders. Zhang, though, does have a connection with Japan: her father, Zhang Shu, was once China’s ambassador in Tokyo.

Many are linking China’s frosty welcome to a simmering row over Taiwan that began shortly after Takaichi made her diplomatic debut at the 2025 Apec summit in South Korea, where she and Xi vowed to build “constructive and stable” relations.

Less than a fortnight later, Takaichi triggered a diplomatic crisis when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan, whose westernmost island, Yonaguni , is just 100km from Taiwan.

Insisting that Japan could exercise its right to collective self-defence – or coming to the aid of an ally, namely the US – Takaichi said Tokyo had to plan for a crisis in the Taiwan strait.

Beijing has not ruled out the use of force to annex Taiwan – a self-governing democracy it regards as a Chinese province – under what it calls “reunification”.

China’s foreign ministry condemned her remarks at the time as “wrongful and dangerous,” while online, many accused Japan’s leader of dragging her country back into prewar militarism.

The dispute soured economic and cultural ties. Beijing warned Chinese citizens not to take holidays or study in Japan , claiming, without evidence, that they would face threats to their safety. Grassroots exchanges were called off and the Chinese releases of Japanese films postponed indefinitely.

Panda diplomacy also took a hit in January, when Xiao Xiao and Lei Lei, a pair of giant pandas that had been kept at Ueno Zoo in Tokyo, departed Japan, leaving the country without one of the animals for the first time since 1972, when Tokyo and Beijing normalised diplomatic ties.

As Xi, Trump and Putin prepared to hold historic three-way talks in Shenzhen on Thursday, Takaichi managed only a cordial handshake and a few words with Xi – another reminder that Japan-China relations have yet to come in from the cold.

stories.title: Google rejects UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
stories.summary: Move comes after Brand's wife shared a message from him in which he claimed his innocence.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 18 November 2026

Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.

The disgraced comedian is in prison after being sentenced to 10-and-a-half years following his conviction for rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Google told BBC News in a statement it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".

It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."

On Sunday, Brand's wife Laura shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.

However, speaking on BBC Breakfast, housing minister Matthew Pennycook described the video as "abhorrent" and said the government remained in "close dialogue" with Google.

Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".

"It relies on YouTube, in this instance ... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.

An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".

Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" that the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.

"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".

Badenoch told Today YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".

"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.

Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".

Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.

In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.

In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, said she found the message shared by Laura Brand on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told the Today programme this week.

She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.

"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision to disable Brand's social media accounts on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.

"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."

The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.

Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.

"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."

stories.title: UK to provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones
stories.summary: The prime minister is set to make the announcement at a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street last month

Published 19 November 2026, 09:10 GMT

The UK will provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones to target Russia beyond the front line, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to announce later.

The drone support will be announced at a meeting in Berlin of Ukraine's allies, the Coalition of the Willing, and is part of a new £260m package to boost its war defences this winter.

The government said the drones are able to fly up to 625 miles (1,000km) and carry heavier warheads, enabling Ukraine to target military production facilities.

The move is the latest sign of a growing British involvement in drone technology for Ukraine. The government said 80% of the package will be spent in the UK.

The Berlin talks come as US President Donald Trump is meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping.

Ahead of that meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in China, Trump said both he and Xi want to see an end to the Ukraine war.

Trump says summit with Xi and Putin in China is 'making history'

In a statement released ahead of the latest meeting of the group of 36 countries committed to supporting Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire or peace agreement - the government said the UK is also building maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to help Ukraine's war effort.

Burnham, who is co-chairing the meeting, said the UK must do everything it can to make sure Ukraine can defend itself from Russian attacks throughout the winter.

The prime minister said: "Plunging millions of Ukrainians into the freezing cold and starving them of heat and warmth won't see Putin win this war, it will only cement our resolve to support Ukraine.

"That is why I am determined the UK will do everything we can to ensure Ukraine is able to defend itself from Russia's barrage of attacks and systematic striking of critical national infrastructure."

Before this latest support package was announced, government figures put the amount of support provided by the UK for Ukraine since Russia invaded the country in February 2022 at £35.5bn. , external

In recent days, Ukraine has struck oil refineries in southern Russia, and has repeatedly hit the Crimean Bridge - a significant logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

Meanwhile, Russian forces have been focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before winter with attacks on critical infrastructure.

The UK is among a number of countries also supplying Ukraine with lightweight missiles which are being used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

Ukraine's strike rate is now close to 70%, more than double what it was just a couple of months ago, Downing Street said.

The UK also pledged further air defence support this week and sanctioned Russia's 10 major oil producers.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the government was delivering on a promise for more support for Ukraine at the Budget.

"Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes," he said.

Meanwhile, on Friday Burnham will head to Brussels for a UK-EU summit, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

stories.title: Leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
stories.summary: The proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will also include capping ground rent at £250.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2026, 02:02 GMT

The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the ownership rules for flats in England and Wales and cap ground rents at £250 a year.

Under the plans, which will not become law until at least next year, most new leasehold flats will eventually be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the 21st century".

But the Residential Freehold Association says the plan is an "unprecedented abuse" of their rights, which will wipe billions from the value of pension funds, which have invested heavily in property.

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, to be published on Thursday, is likely to contain further details on when the measures would come into force.

In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months.

'Continuous torture cell'

The bill will also include plans to cap ground rent - the annual fee paid by current leaseholders to their freeholder - at £250 from 2028. That will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.

Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.

Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.

The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.

But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".

Fozia Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again

When she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.

However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.

Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.

Scotland does not have leasehold tenures, while Northern Ireland has just a handful of leasehold properties.

The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other other countries around the world, which do not have leaseholds.

It comes as more than 1,000 leaseholders have contacted the BBC over the past two years with complaints about the current system.

Risk of two-tier system

Campaigners have welcomed many of the reforms, but questioned what happens to the millions of people who already own leasehold homes.

While the legislation is expected to reshape ownership for new developments, converting existing leasehold buildings into commonhold is far more complicated. And it has led to concerns that current leaseholders will be left behind.

Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system of those buying new homes and existing leaseholders.

He began campaigning on behalf of flat owners following the Grenfell Tower tragedy. He says: "It's so complicated, will the measures that are being introduced actually benefit everyone?"

Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system

The government says the bill will make it easier for existing leaseholders to convert to commonhold, abolish forfeiture - so people cannot lose their homes over relatively small debts - improve transparency around service charges and crack down on estate charges.

Pennycook says it will transform "the experience of homeownership for existing leaseholders by giving them greater rights and protections and providing them with easy and effective escape routes".

However, the issue about how existing leaseholders can move into commonhold and how freeholders should be compensated remains unresolved.

stories.body:
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours

In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power” .

Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.

In Donald Trump , Putin has a ready supplier of balm to soothe his injured vanity. The US president has a shallow, venal concept of power. He is impressed by gilded palaces and heavily armed thugs. He feels thwarted by American democracy and envies tyrants who operate without equivalent restraint. Since Trump measures greatness in a country by its leader’s contempt for smaller nations and appetite for self-enriching plunder, he willingly promotes Russia back to the top tier.

That is the significance to Putin of a three-way summit with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. It confers trappings of parity with the world’s two genuine superpowers. That is a win for Russia, regardless of whether anything of substance is agreed.

The agenda is vague. The Chinese foreign ministry has said the discussion will focus on “ safeguarding world peace ” and “promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”. Xi will be satisfied with the projection of China as convener of a new world order. Trump has said he expects the conversation to cover denuclearisation, Iran, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”.

The image of three leaders calibrating the balance of global power has been compared to Yalta, February 1945: Roosevelt, Stalin and Churchill drawing up plans for postwar Europe . That was a week-long conference where military allies were settling the fate of a defeated enemy. The analogy is revealing mostly as an expression of anxiety in those who will not be present.

For many Europeans, Yalta conjures memories of cynical partition, with eastern nations condemned to decades of Soviet captivity. The fear in Kyiv is that Putin will use his privileged access to Trump’s ear to pour in poisonous theories about the origins of the Ukraine war and how to end it – a twisted narrative of Nato provocation, irresistible Russian superiority and the need for Europe to stop wasting money and US military hardware on a losing cause.

The exclusion of European democracies from the room in Shenzhen is partly just a function of the conversation happening on the sidelines of a summit for countries with Pacific coasts. But it probes a deep strategic insecurity. Ukraine’s continental allies have asserted their rights to be part of any peace process but not found a way to turn that entitlement into a collective position, coordinated by a figure with diplomatic gravitas.

After a round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Jared Kushner, one of Trump’s envoys, made the reassuring statement that a deal could not be done “without Europeans being at the table”. By contrast, Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, accused the Europeans of lacking serious intent to find solutions. He dismissed their delegation to the Gulf as “tourists” who might as well “chat in the hotel bar”.

That is standard Kremlin trolling, but it cuts with a shard of truth. It points to an old problem, often described with the apocryphal tale of Henry Kissinger complaining that there was no number to call when he wanted to speak to Europe. The challenge is more acute today. The institutional and economic foundations of European influence are under assault. Trump is ambivalent at best about Nato. His administration is protectionist and nationalist. Maga ideology casts liberal democratic Europe as a moribund civilisation erasing itself with mass immigration.

China treats Europe as a bundle of consumers for manufactured exports whose politicians usually, by default, defer to Washington. The EU has ambitions of “strategic autonomy” but the process is slow and expensive. It means evolution from soft power – rivalling the US and China in economic heft as a single market whose regulations set global standards – to something a lot harder. European electorates may despise Trump and fear Putin, but they are not all comfortable with the choices that follow if the remedy is a shift in budget priorities to higher defence spending.

A lot of European politics in recent years has been driven with a longing eye on the rear view mirror, wondering if there is a way back to the old world of open trade, respect for international law, a White House that wouldn’t abet the Kremlin in an imperial land grab. But there is growing recognition that Europe’s future cannot resemble its recent past.

The UK is part of that story, and Andy Burnham has understood the implications. In a speech on Monday , the prime minister expanded his criticism of Brexit from the economic to the geopolitical arena. It was, he said, “the first domino to fall” in a pattern of global fragmentation. It introduced a schism in European alliances that was “exactly what our enemies wanted”. Burnham’s audit of the costs in forfeited trade was familiar enough, but he moved the argument up a gear by noting that withdrawal from the top table of European decision-making has cost Britain power and influence in the world. That is something continuity Brexiters cannot compute.

after newsletter promotion

As Burnham finds his pro-European voice, the old Eurosceptic myth-making industrial complex is grinding back into motion. Newspapers have published tenuous stories about the cost of restored alignment with Brussels and hypothetical migrant influxes. Veterans of the leave campaign are limbering up for a dismal dance around the 2016 totem pole. It is rotten from exposure to a decade of international storms.

Britain is a regional power that undervalued the amplifying effect of EU membership. The benefits of being in the club felt enough like great-power status to fool Eurosceptics into thinking they could go it alone. They cling to that delusion. Kemi Badenoch has written about Britain having “latent great power attributes”. She doesn’t have a theory of how those dormant traits will be awoken in a world carved into continental blocs.

Burnham’s plan is hardly precise, but at least he starts with facts: Britain is a European country; Europe will be safer and richer if it pools its resources; the UK should not want to be on the margin.

A summit where Xi, Putin and Trump claim to be deciding the fate of the world may not yield much in the way of concrete deals, but it still contains a warning to European democracies. And a choice. One option is to boost leverage through closer continental cooperation. The alternative is flight into fantasies of immaculate national sovereignty and resurrected historical grandeur. One of those routes is a way for Europe to grow autonomy, security and prosperity in the 21st century. The other is the path of bitter self-defeat modelled by Brexit .

Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy

Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January

Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices increased and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September and was in line with City economists’ forecasts.

As households brace for the colder winter months with household gas and electricity costs soaring, the latest figures push the headline inflation rate to the highest level in a year.

In a reading underscoring the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates, the ONS said fuel prices were the major contributor. Annual costs of raw materials and goods leaving factories also continued to climb, driven by rising energy and crude oil prices amid the Iran war.

Fuel prices for motorists rose at an annual rate of 33.2%, the largest increase since July 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sparked a global surge in energy prices.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p a litre between September and October to reach 174.7p a litre, the highest level in four years. Diesel prices rose by 7p a litre to 199.5p a litre, the highest price on records dating back to 1996.

Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide.

At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20m households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm.

The latest inflation figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October.

A forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight on Wednesday predicted a 26% jump in energy bills in Great Britain from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.

Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Earlier this month, Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the longer the conflict continued the more likely it was that rate increases would be needed, despite a recent drop in global energy prices since the US midterm elections.

Speaking at a conference in London on Tuesday, Bailey said inflation was “probably going to be a bit less” than the 5% forecast made by the Bank earlier this month.

after newsletter promotion

However, he said that if the war pushed energy prices higher, the “more likely persistent inflationary effects will take hold and the higher the level of interest rates will need to be”.

Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year. Analysts said the Bank could raise borrowing costs from as early as next month.

Core inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – was unchanged at 2.8%, matching economists’ forecasts. Services inflation, which the Bank has been monitoring closely for evidence of domestic inflationary pressures becoming entrenched, also held steady at 3.7%, slightly below City predictions for a rate of 3.8%.

Air fares rose by 1.8% between September and October amid an increase in long-haul ticket prices – offset by a downward effect from European flights. Prices for alcohol and tobacco also rose, by 4.5%, influenced by the timing of an increase in tobacco duty at the start of the month.

Food prices rose at the slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September.

Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said: “The conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world.

“The household energy payment, announced in our budget, is providing £100 directly into 20 million bank accounts in January, which will help to give families breathing space now.

“The budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future.”

stories.body:
Introduction: Anthropic's record IPO ahead of today's stock market float

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of the world’s biggest stock market listing, and other events across business, the financial markets and the world economy.

We’re going to see the biggest initial public offering in history today; Anthropic is floating on the US stock market, in what will be a major test for the market’s enthusiasm for the AI industry.

Despite fears that AI may be a bubble, primed to pop, Anthropic – the frontier AI firm behind the Claude chatbot – has seen a surge of demand from investors looking to buy a stake.

Last night, Anthropic announced it had raised a record-breaking sum from its IPO. In a sign of strong demand, the company increased the price at which its selling its shares to $83, up from a previous guide of $70-$78.

That will raise $81.3bn (£61.8bn), exceeding the $75bn raised by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June .

If you include another $26bn raised through a private sale of shares to tech firms, Anthropic’s IPO has secured a record sum of $107.3bn, Sky News has calculated .

Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei and his fellow co-founders are expected to ring the Nasdaq opening bell at 9.30am New York time (2.30pm in the UK).

The company will then make its debut on the Nasdaq under the symbol “ANT”, although we may have to wait a little while before its shares start trading.

Anthropic joins the market at a time when the Nvidia crisis has rattled investors. Tech stocks have dropped in recent weeks, pulling the Nasdaq Composite down by over 10% from its record high at the start of October.

The IPO will value Anthropic at around $1.5tn (£1.1tn), placing it around 12th on the list of the world’s biggest companies .

That’s despite the company being loss-making; in 2025 it posted an operating loss of over $8bn, as expenses (nearly $13bn) outpaced revenues ($4.6bn).

Revenues have accelerated in 2026, though, but the company’s challenge is to a) maintain this, and b) turn it into profits.

Garry White, chief investment commentator at wealth manager Raymond James, explains:

double quotation mark “Anthropic’s IPO should be a clear litmus test of current market sentiment towards the AI investment boom. If the shares enjoy a strong post-listing rally, it would signal that markets remain convinced a handful of AI leaders can eventually generate profits large enough to justify today’s vast spending on talent, infrastructure and computing power. “Conversely, a weak reception or a sharp decline after flotation could suggest investors are becoming more selective, drawing a distinction between AI’s transformative potential and the commercial challenge of converting rapid revenue growth into sustainable earnings.

The agenda

10am GMT: A French government bond auction

1.30pm GMT: US initial jobless claims data

2.30pm GMT: Wall Street trading begins

Anthropic's shares expected to pop when trading begins

There’s just 90 minutes to go until the US stock market opens for trading.

Despite lifting the price of its IPO yesterday, to $83 a share, Anthropic is still expected to jump in value once its stock starts trading.

That means we should see the traditional ‘pop’ when a new company joins the stock market, and investors who missed out on the sale process try to buy in.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at investing and trading platform IG , has the details:

double quotation mark “IG’s pre-IPO market for Anthropic has seen a notable bounce since Nvidia’s results as sentiment towards tech and AI becomes more enthusiastic as the Jensen scandal settles down. From a low of $97 earlier in the week IG clients expect the stock to easily top $100 in initial trading and continue to gain. With the price now trading at $105, the AI giant would be valued at $1.9 trillion, just shy of the magic $2 trillion mark that had initially been mooted when the IPO plans first became widespread news. Markets needed reassurance that the AI trade still has plenty of life left in it, and it looks like the Anthropic IPO will do just that.”

Reminder: Anthropic’s float is going to be the biggest IPO of all time , as it will rake in $83.1bn through its share sale, giving a valuation of $1.5tn.

Such was the demand for shares that investors at Hargreaves Lansdown only received a third of their order.

And as flagged earlier , its shares were up 20% in ‘grey market’ trading this morning.

The Anthropic IPO has already been rather lucrative for Wall Street banks – who will be paid $550m for their work on the float.

That’s according to Bloomberg , who explain :

double quotation mark The artificial intelligence lab agreed to pay the banks, led by Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley, a fee of nearly 68 basis points according to Anthropic’s latest filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, roughly in line with the SpaceX banks’ share of its offering. The haul would be larger than the $500 million the banks were paid for SpaceX in its $86.2 billion IPO.

Dan Ives , partner and senior managing director at Y orkville Ives + Co , is encouraged by the demand for Anthropic shares:

double quotation mark “This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors.”

US shopping giant Walmart has just raised its annual targets, a little.

The retailer now expects net sales to grow by between 4.9% to 5.2% this financial year, up from its previous forecast of 4% to 5%.

It also posted a 5.2% rise in revenues in the last quarter, to $188.8bn, and a 16% rise in operating income.

FTSE 100 hits six-week low as Anthropic hogs the limelight

Anthropic’s IPO has not brought much cheer to the London stock market today.

The FTSE 100 index of blue-chip shares has slipped to a six-week low, down 39 points (-0.37%) at 10,512 points, as investors favour technology stocks instead today.

Fallers in London include investment bank Investec (-5.5%), retail group JD Sports (-4.2%), and energy company National Grid (-2.5%).

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, says:

double quotation mark The London index is in the shade as investors’ interest is consumed by the Anthropic market debut and big tech once again steals the limelight on global markets. The swell of enthusiasm around Anthropic’s stock market debut is meanwhile creating a rising tide of optimism towards big tech. With the IPO reportedly up to ten times oversubscribed and the offer price coming in at $83, above initial expectations, demand appears to be running hot. The Nasdaq is set for a strong start to trading, with appetite seemingly returning for US technology giants. Even beleaguered chip giant Nvidia looks set to claw back some ground.

2026 has not been a blowout year for stock market listings in London.

But some companies are still interested in listing here. Yesterday, British cancer drug developer Ellipses Pharma said it was exploring a London listing through a reverse takeover of special purpose acquisition company Wolfram Resources .

Wolfram explained:

double quotation mark If completed, the Proposed Acquisition would give the Company and its shareholders exposure to a portfolio of clinical and near-clinical oncology assets with an attractive growth profile, while providing Ellipses with a public markets platform and access to additional capital to support the continued development of its pipeline

Anthropic’s IPO will mean that that personal pensions (such as SIPPs), and stocks and shares accounts (ISAs), will have more exposure to the AI industry.

Professor Richard Whittle, professor of artificial intelligence (ai) and public policy at the University of Salford, explains:

double quotation mark “This record listing shows a continuation of AI exuberance that may bring a tipping point closer. In the near term, it refinances activity, gives early investors a public price and clears the path for OpenAI’s expected debut next year. “However, the AI bet has moved from a small circle of private backers to the public. Up to a fifth of the shares were reserved for retail investors. A private valuation is revised infrequently according to detailed analysis and evaluation. A listed share is repriced every day, indeed every minute, and each quarterly report, profit announcement or scandal, becomes a public test of whether the imagined AI future is still believed. “Bubbles don’t burst on the day of the largest deal. They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect. Today’s IPO pushes the AI boom along, it also puts its future into the hands of a far greater number of more risk averse investors who will quickly sell if their FOMO [fear of missing out] turns to a fear of losing their money.”

Anthropic is the first major frontier AI model developer to go public, and it’s coming to market at an interesting time.

The Democratic Party’s success in the US midterm elections earlier this month have hit AI stocks, on fears that data centre rollouts will face more opposition.

Today’s IPO also follows months of warnings that AI valuations have risen too high.

Alexander Lis , CIO at investment firm SDV , reckons Anthropic’s IPO looks “quite rushed”, and cites a few possible explanations:

The company may fear there won’t be enough demand later, as investors have grown tired of new listings.

They may see problems with their performance on the horizon, for example, due to competition from other models.

Investors in private markets have lost patience and are ready to get liquidity at almost any cost.

European stock markets are inching higher today.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index is up 0.2% this morning, rising from the three-week low hit yesterday.

How Anthropic warned AI could be an existential risk

When companies try to float on the stock market, they usually devote a lot of time persuading investors what a great opportunity they are.

Anthropic did that too, of course! They argued that frontier intelligence “represents a larger opportunity than any prior technology cycle”, and could accelerating progress in scientific research, such as drug discovery, and speed up economic growth.

More unusually, though, Anthropic devoted 90 pages – around a quarter of its SEC filing – to outlining all the risks it faces.

It started by warning of the risk that its AI models go rogue:

double quotation mark Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Before flagging the danger that AI creates a catastrophe, saying:

double quotation mark Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.

Anthropic has sold $1.1bn (£836m) worth of stock to retail investors in the UK and continental Europe through its IPO, Bloomberg has calculated.

It says :

double quotation mark The artificial intelligence lab sold just over 3.6 million shares to retail investors in the UK and close to 9.7 million shares to those in the European Union, Norway and Switzerland, according to regulatory filings reviewed by Bloomberg News…. At the IPO price of $83 per share, the company and its founders raised about $300 million and $801 million, respectively, through the dedicated offerings in Britain and on the continent.
