Closing post

Time to wrap up

Jensen Huang has thrown his hat into the ring to return to his role running Nvidia, less than a week after being ousted amid an alleged spy scandal.

Huang has issued a statement admitting making “serious mistakes” in his personal life – a nod to his previous admission of cheating on his wife, allegedly with a suspected Chinese spy.

He says:

double quotation mark I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.

But Huang also indicated he would be happy to return to his role, saying:

double quotation mark Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Here’s the full story:

Huang , and Nvidia’s top lawyer, have agreed to testify to Congressional committees next month .

Stock markets have fallen across Europe and in New York, ahead of Nvidia’s results after today’s closing Wall Street bell.

The tech-focused Nasdaq led the fallers, down 1.6%.

In London, the FTSE 100 posted its biggest one-day fall since March, falling by 1.76%.

Investors are eager to hear tonight whether Nvidia is sticking to its financial guidance, following the scandal which forced out CEO Jensen Huang last week.

The company has already announced the creation of a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee , to keep tabs on its operations.

Two US departments have confirmed that Megaspeed is being investigated for violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia’s chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

China has hit back after the US closed a loophole which allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia-powered data centres in third-party countries.

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would take “necessary measures” to safeguard its own interests, saying:

double quotation mark “The US has repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security, abused export controls and even interfered in China’s normal trade and technological cooperation with other countries, unjustifiably suppressing the development of China’s high-tech industries.”

Why Huang should not be reinstated

Jensen Huang should not be reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO, argues Jeffrey Sonnenfeld , the Lester Crown Professor of Leadership Practice at the Yale School of Management .

Writing in Time Magazine today , Sonnenfeld argues that Nvidia’s board were wise to closed the door on Huang’s return, and shouldn’t let it be forced open again.

Sonnenfeld writes:

double quotation mark That door should stay shut. Over 33 years, Huang built the company at the center of the AI era, but in our view, his conduct nevertheless made his position untenable. He misled directors about undisclosed relationships and oversaw a firm no one could check—a breakdown in trust that was magnified in China, where he advocated loosening export controls even as restricted chips reached Chinese military units and a Shanghai facility tied to Alice Huang’s network. The political push to restore him rests on the billions his most prominent advocates have riding on his customer-financing web and on misleading geopolitical spin, at the expense of genuine shareholder concerns and national defense.

Sonnenfeld also argues that a board that can be overruled by a petition has “no function”, concluding:

double quotation mark Nvidia’s directors deferred to Huang for years and intervened late, and reversing course under outside pressure now would merely extend a habit of deference. Instead, the board should let its investigation finish, restore standalone Singapore revenue disclosures, and select a successor on the merits. Huang spent 33 years building an enterprise the AI era cannot do without. Now comes the defining test of a great company—whether it can outlast the person who built it.

FTSE 100 posts biggest drop since March

London’s stock market has just recorded its biggest one-day drop since the first month of the Iran war.

The FTSE 100 share index has closed down 191.68 points, or -1.76%, at 10,689 points.

That’s its biggest percentage drop since 19 March this year.

Jensen Huang: I love our country, and I love Nvidia

Here’s the full statement issued by Jensen Huang , signalling he would like to return to his former job running Nvidia .

double quotation mark Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

This is quite the intervention from Jensen Huang , just five hours before Nvidia is due to release its latest financial results.

It makes it harder for the company’s board to avoid questions about its succession plans, and heaps the pressuer on interim CEO Colette Kress to calm investors’ nerves about the company’s outlook.

Jensen Huang says he is prepared to return as Nvidia CEO

Newsflash: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has issued a statement saying he would be “honoured” to return to the role, less than a week after resigning.

In a statement issued to the media, Huang – whe quit last week over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy – says:

double quotation mark “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret.

Last weekend, an open letter called on Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation was conducted.

Today, Huang says:

double quotation mark “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

However, Nvidia’s board indicated yesterday they are not considering reinstating Huang as CEO….

Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer at International Services, says Nvidia is confronting several crises at once:

An employee rebellion: Growing internal pressure to bring Huang back, with warnings that critical AI talent could walk away.

A leadership vacuum: Can Kress reassure investors, customers and employees while the board searches for a permanent CEO?

A Wall Street confidence test: Will strong earnings be enough to stabilize the stock, or has the leadership crisis fundamentally changed Nvidia’s valuation?

Washington and China: New scrutiny of Nvidia’s China-related business and national security questions adds another layer of uncertainty.

The future of AI: Could a prolonged crisis at the world’s leading AI chipmaker disrupt investment, innovation and the companies dependent on Nvidia’s technology?

Nearly every stock on the FTSE 100 share index is in the red today – pulling the Footsie down by 176 points, or 1.6%, to 10,707 points in late trading.

Nasdaq hits eight-month low

The US technology stock index, the Nasdaq Composite, has just hit an eight-month low, down around 1.6%.

Markets fall ahead of Nvidia's results

Stock markets on both sides of the Atlantic are dropping deeper into the red.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average is now down 1%, having lost 511 points to around 51,096 points.

And in London, the FTSE 100 index is down 1.4%, having dropped by 154 points to 10,726 points.

Investors may be getting jittery ahead of Nvidia’s results tonight, to be followed by Anthropic’s IPO on Thursday.

Reminder: Wall Street will hear from Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress , tonight, following the resignation of Jensen Huang last week after allegations that he conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Nvidia will also face questions about claims that billions of dollars of its chips were sold to China, and about the implications of the US closing a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia -powered data centres in other countries.

Joe Mazzola , head trading & derivatives strategist at Charles Schwab, says:

double quotation mark The chip giant typically releases results about half an hour after the close. Nvidia’s call follows at 5 p.m. ET, led by CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress. If a board member or executive besides Kress speaks prominently, speculation might rise about where they stand in the Huang succession stakes. Investors could hear plenty of scuttlebutt on the CEO topic after the call. The biggest question is whether Nvidia can keep growing parabolically without Huang at the helm. Outlook is paramount, and a devastating outcome would be if Nvidia pulls guidance. Back in August, Nvidia forecast fiscal 2028 revenue growth of 70%. See if the company sticks to that. Export controls on advanced chips are another topic, especially after the U.S. took new measures to limit remote access to advanced AI chips. Shares fell more than 4% Monday as investors prepared for worst-case scenarios, and big share moves are priced in for Nvidia depending on the outcome. If the call gets an optimistic take, the entire sector could feel relief. Though quarterly results might seem secondary, earnings are seen up 90.4% to $2.48 per share and revenue is seen up 91.3% to $109.1 billion.

stories.title: Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
stories.summary: In her decision, Judge Emma Kelly says there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The injunction granted by the High Court prevents Ryan Bridge and Raise the Colours from attaching flags and other items to public property

Published 18 November 2026

Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.

The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.

Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.

The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.

The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.

The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.

Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.

The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.

The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire, where the county council secured a permanent injunction against four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.

Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge had argued an injunction would breach the European Convention on Human Rights

Bridge opposed the injunction, arguing it would interfere with rights to freedom of expression and protest under the European Convention on Human Rights.

His barrister, Liam Wells, told the court the campaign amounted to political expression protected by the convention and argued the injunction would have a "chilling effect" on those rights.

In her ruling, Kelly stressed the order was not a ban on displaying flags.

"The interim injunction needs to be understood for what it is," she said.

"It is not the court nor the claimant 'banning the union jack' or the display of Pride flags or anything of the like.

"Whilst the interim injunction order will cover flags of all types, it is limited in scope to the restraint of unauthorised flags attached to highway street furniture or infrastructure, and to the restraint of associated conduct, within the administrative area of Birmingham."

She added that concerns the injunction would unduly restrict free expression were "unwarranted" and said she was satisfied it was "just and convenient" to grant the order.

The council said anyone who breaches the injunction could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court

The injunction covers all unauthorised flags attached to street furniture, regardless of the type of flag involved.

Birmingham City Council's cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, welcomed the ruling and described it as an "important step" in tackling unauthorised attachments to public highways.

She said residents remained free to display flags on their own property and said the council's approach had been "proportionate and evidence-led".

Councillor Jane Baston called the interim injunction an "important step" for the authority

Councillor Robert Alden, leader of Birmingham local Conservatives, criticised the authority's decision to pursue the injunction, saying it should focus on resolving the city's bin strike and improving basic services.

Campaign group Brummies United Against Racism & Hate Crime welcomed the ruling, describing it as "a welcome decision and long overdue".

A further hearing is due to take place in Birmingham on Thursday.

stories.title: Trump admin orders Kalshi to halt wagers on what words Trump will say
stories.summary: CFTC: Kalshi bets may violate US ban on contracts that can be easily manipulated.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
CFTC: Kalshi bets may violate US ban on contracts that can be easily manipulated.

The Trump administration ordered prediction market Kalshi to stop offering event contracts that pay out based on whether President Trump will say a specific word before a particular date. Kalshi halted trading in the contracts while the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) conducts a review into whether the Trump mention contracts violate federal law.

CNBC reported yesterday that “Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of ‘mention’ contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC.” Kalshi told media outlets that it is complying with the CFTC order.

The markets taken down by Kalshi allowed users to wager on whether Trump would say certain words, including nicknames and the names of countries and companies. A similar expired event contract that can still be viewed on Kalshi’s website asked whether Trump would use the nicknames “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” “Sleepy Joe,” and “Whack Job” or “Wack Job” before April 2026.

The CFTC order issued to Kalshi last week applies broadly to “the TRUMPSAY contract series.” The event contracts in this series include trades in the format, “Will [word] be said by Donald Trump after Issuance and before [date]?” The CFTC order also applied to a specific event contract that asks, “What nicknames will Trump say before 2027?”

Trump teleprompter aide bet on what Trump would say

The CFTC order came several months after the federal agency settled charges against a Trump teleprompter aide who made over $100,000 in Kalshi wagers on what Trump would say in prepared remarks. On August 28, the CFTC required the man, Gabriel Perez, to disgorge profits of $107,539.02 and pay a civil penalty of $65,000.

“In his position, Perez had access to presidential speeches prior to those speeches being delivered and Perez misappropriated that information—in breach of his duty of trust and confidence—to trade presidential mention market contracts, generating over $107,500 in profits,” the CFTC said at the time.

Senate Democrats recently said the White House hasn’t taken meaningful action against insider trading, “all while the president and his family stand to personally profit from their participation in prediction markets.” Prediction markets have flourished under the Trump administration’s permissive regulatory approach. The CFTC has allowed prediction markets to offer sports gambling nationwide and filed lawsuits against states that attempt to regulate Kalshi under their gambling laws.

Kalshi recently dropped Donald Trump Jr. as an advisor , saying it made the decision because Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm increased its investment in its competitor, Polymarket. Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour also acknowledged that the “optics” of Trump Jr.’s advisory role weren’t good for Kalshi. Trump Jr. still stands to benefit from Kalshi’s success, because he was given equity shares in the company.

The CFTC has said that mention markets are easily manipulated but reviews them on a case-by-case basis instead of prohibiting them. Prediction markets can “self-certify” that any new event contract complies with US law and start offering it without waiting for the CFTC’s permission, but the CFTC can halt trading afterward based on reviews of specific contracts.

CFTC: Kalshi did not comply with advisory

The Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) prohibits the listing of contracts that are readily susceptible to manipulation. CFTC staff issued a September advisory about the legality of markets on what people will say, and whether they will attend an event or interact with another person. The advisory said these contracts may be viewed as “presumptively readily susceptible to manipulation,” because they “may be controlled by a single individual, a small group of individuals, or persons with access to or influence over the individual whose words, attendance, or interaction determines settlement.”

The CFTC said this type of contract requires measures “to prevent manipulation and misappropriation of material non-public information,” and that Kalshi failed to comply with the CFTC staff advisory. About “a week after the Staff Advisory was released, Kalshi listed the Contract [on nicknames] for trading without amending the [TRUMPSAY] Contract Series’ self-certification (or submitting a new self-certification) to make the ‘heightened showing’ of non-manipulability required by the Staff Advisory,” the order said.

The CFTC said it will conduct “a proceeding to determine whether the certification of the Contracts was false—that is, whether the Contracts comply with the Act, including the Core Principles , and Commission regulations thereunder as Kalshi has certified.” So far, “Kalshi has not adequately demonstrated that the Contracts are not readily susceptible to manipulation” as required by law, the order said.

“Given the available supporting evidence, including that Kalshi has not attempted to establish that the Contracts are non-manipulable with respect to the Staff Advisory’s guidance, the Commission presumptively believes the certification is false,” the order said.

Kalshi CEO: What Trump says “moves markets”

The CFTC order is not a determination on whether the Trump mention markets can meet the standard of not being readily susceptible to manipulation. Rather, it is a determination that Kalshi has so far failed to show that the contracts are not easily manipulated.

The order “resolves only that, based on the current record, Kalshi has not demonstrated that the Contracts as certified comply with the Act and that the Contracts should not trade while the Commission completes its review,” the CFTC said.

We contacted Kalshi and will update this article if it provides a response.

Mansour defended the Trump mention contracts at an Axios event on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg . “What the president does say moves markets,” Mansour said. “So predicting what he’s about to say is actually pretty meaningful.”

The Bloomberg article noted that “Kalshi’s main rival Polymarket still has live mention markets tied to Trump’s speeches on its international website, which is not regulated by the CFTC.” Polymarket offers a separate US-regulated version of its prediction market.

stories.title: Lammy urges Burnham to take UK back into the EU
stories.summary: The former deputy PM's intervention comes after Burnham reopened a debate over the UK's long-term future.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 18 November 2026

David Lammy has urged Andy Burnham to take Labour into the next general election with a pledge to rejoin the European Union.

The former deputy prime minister's intervention comes as Burnham prepares to explain how he sees the UK's long-term relationship with Europe developing.

Burnham confirmed on Tuesday he plans to set out his options next month, in the wake of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday.

Former business secretary Peter Kyle echoed Lammy's call to rejoin, meaning four former ministers from Sir Keir Starmer's cabinet have now publicly supported reversing Brexit in recent weeks.

The prime minister has held out the possibility he could ask to rejoin at some stage, whilst ruling out major changes before the next election.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves said earlier this month she believed "Britain's future lies in the European Union", following ex-Welsh secretary Jo Stevens in saying she wanted the UK to become an EU member again.

Neither specified a timeframe for the move, with Reeves insisting it was important to "get the next steps right".

But Lammy has now gone further, calling for Burnham to advocate rejoining at the next election, paving the way for a negotiation on a deal to return.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, he added that the public should then be given a vote on whether to accept the new membership deal.

Returning to the bloc's customs union, in which EU member states charge the same taxes on imported goods, would not deliver "enough" economic growth, he said.

He added that rejoining Europe's single market from the outside was "not a runner" as it would mean applying swathes of EU law without a say on the content.

Another cabinet minister under Sir Keir Starmer, Peter Kyle, has also backed this approach, writing on Substack , external earlier that a "complex halfway option" would be "the worst of all worlds".

He added that a promise to rejoin at the next election, followed by a renegotiation and a referendum on the final terms, was the "only way through I see".

He added: "How would I vote? Well, I would want to see the deal before deciding. I want Britain back in the EU, but not at any cost."

Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship Published 1 day ago

The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left Published 1 day ago

Lammy, who is also a former foreign secretary, argued the UK would be able to rejoin the EU whilst staying outside the passport-free Schengen travel zone and without committing to adopt the euro.

But he appeared to concede that Britain's EU budget rebate, first negotiated in the 1980s, could become less financially generous, adding that a "different formula" for financial contributions would be "up for negotiation".

He also revealed he had made an unsuccessful attempt to persuade Sir Keir to "tear up" his red lines on Europe towards the end of his two-year premiership, but the former prime minister had encountered resistance from within his cabinet.

Labour's 2024 election manifesto committed the party to "make Brexit work" whilst ruling out rejoining either its customs union or single market.

Any move away from those red lines by Burnham would set up a huge dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at the next election.

But Lammy argued the prime minister's status as a former mayor from the north of England meant he was "uniquely placed" to convince the public of the need to reverse the decision to leave.

'Long and painful'

It comes as Burnham prepares to travel to the Brussels this Friday for an EU summit at which both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

The prime minister inherited negotiations on those deals from his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who kicked off talks on the agreements last year.

But he has also started a broader discussion over the UK's long-term relationship with Europe, which has been welcomed by some within his own party but seen him accused by critics of betraying the result of the 2016 decision to leave.

Burnham's Conservative predecessor Lord Cameron, who resigned as prime minister after losing the 2016 Brexit referendum, has urged the Labour leader not to start a renewed debate over EU membership.

Speaking last week, he warned a fresh debate over the issue would be "long and painful" and could harm attempts to improve upon the exit deal negotiated under the Conservatives.

He added: "The EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."

stories.title: Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report
stories.summary: The prime minister tells the BBC he wants to get "stuck in" after the Milburn report proposes wide-ranging changes to help unemployed young people.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

'I know actually what does work': Burnham unveils 45-day work placement plan for young people

Published 18 November 2026

The prime minister has said he wants to "move quickly" on implementing recommendations in Alan Milburn's report on work and young people.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Andy Burnham said: "This isn't about waiting forever and a long-off-promised reform, I want to get stuck into it right now."

Milburn's report , external urged more job support for under-25s, a shake-up of the benefits system, early intervention in schools and tax cuts for businesses hiring young people.

The government said it backed the review's principles and is expected to set out which proposals it will take on shortly.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was no need for "costly government schemes to fix Labour's own mistakes".

"We need to stop making it so expensive and risky to hire young people," she added.

Last year, the government asked Milburn, a former Labour minister, to do a review into the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), which has now reached almost one million.

Burnham praised the report as a "landmark moment" adding: "This is not just a benefits reform, it's a whole society change he is calling for."

He said he wanted to get the benefit bill down adding: "No one can be comfortable with the idea of hundreds of thousands of young people on benefits - nobody, not me, not anyone."

However, he added that it required "more than the crude cuts the other parties are offering".

"All of my experience says a 'names not numbers' approach that looks at the whole person, their housing, their debt, their mental health issues and creates a rounded response, that is proven to be more successful at getting people into work."

Asked what the number of young people not in education, employment or training should be by the next election, Burnham said he wanted the level to come down "as soon as possible".

He said he wanted 45-day work placements offered to every 16-18-year-old "who wants one" and was working on funding the places.

Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform Published 1 day ago

Milburn says his proposals could save as much as £13.8bn in welfare costs over the next 10 years.

But after the extra spending on support for young people is taken into account, they are only projected to save £200m a year of taxpayers' money overall by 2036 .

During Prime Minister's Questions, Badenoch challenged Burnham over how long the plans would take to produce savings.

"[The prime minister] isn't planning any savings for 10 years," the Conservative leader said.

"We can't wait 10 years. Those young people need those jobs now."

Burnham insisted he would work "as quickly as possible to get the welfare bill down".

The prime minister added that he had asked the cabinet to "reprioritise spending plans" for next year to start funding new work placements for young people.

Accusing the Conservatives of a "cuts-only approach", he said: "The Milburn report says to reduce the welfare bill, you have to improve support."

Meanwhile, the government has also announced it will fully fund college places for everyone aged 16 to 18 in England for 2027/28.

The Association of Colleges said the money would allow its members to enrol thousands of extra students each year "confident in the knowledge that they will receive funding for them".

College funding in England is lagged, so colleges receive money every September for the students they enrolled in the previous September.

Colleges say more teenagers in the population and greater demand for vocational courses means they currently either take on more students than they receive funding for, or they have to turn students away.

However, the DfE does not collect data on how often this happens or how many of those students end up among the 150,000 16 to 18-year-olds who are not in education, employment or training (Neet).

Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's plans help you? Published 1 day ago

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 2 days ago

Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 1 day ago

In his report, Milburn warned that employer National Insurance, wage costs, business rates and employment protections could be factors in deterring employers from hiring unexperienced young people.

"Fair pay, greater security and predictable hours matter," Milburn said, but added that the cost and complexity of hiring young people had increased "sharply".

On workers' rights, Burnham argued a balance had to be struck adding: "The more you strengthen employment security that creates more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in."

Asked if former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had made the situation worse by increasing the tax employers pay, the prime minister said the government had increased support for those hiring long-term unemployed people.

He also defended his reset with the EU, which could make it easier for young Europeans to work in the UK.

He argued that a closer relationship with the EU would help grow the economy, which would provide more opportunities for young people.

Attempts to change the welfare system under Sir Keir Starmer last year failed when Labour backbenchers refused to support the £5bn cuts to benefits, raising concerns about the impact on disabled people.

So far, there are few signs that Burnham's plans will trigger a similar backlash, although some Labour backbenchers and the Unison trade union have said the proposals on benefits could push young people into poverty.

Steve Darling, the Liberal Democrat work and pensions spokesman, said the government should "scrap the damaging job tax" and work with European countries to grow the economy.

Green Party MP Sian Berry urged the minister to "reject cuts" for young disabled people.

"One million young people need a leg up - one that does not come with the chair being kicked out from under them," she said.

Reform UK said immigration was the "elephant in the room" and called on the government to cut employer national insurance for British workers "so that young Brits are at the front of the queue for new jobs".

stories.title: Home secretary plans to tackle 'corrosive' perception of two-tier policing
stories.summary: Shabana Mahmood announces stronger guidance on police impartiality in a speech to police chiefs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 November 2026

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced stronger guidance on police impartiality to tackle what she called the "corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing".

Speaking at a conference of police chiefs on Wednesday, she said "there have been examples of differential treatment" by officers that have allowed "some to whip up the false idea that there is two-tier policing in this country".

Recent complaints about alleged two-tier policing have mostly come from those on the right in politics.

They have pointed to the arrest of Henry Nowak as he was dying after being stabbed by Vickrum Digwa who had accused him of racism.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued that white people are treated differently by police because of their race. But critics say this claim risks overlooking the long‑standing experiences of black and minority ethnic communities.

Some senior police figures have also strongly rejected the claim of two-tier policing.

Mahmood began her speech by hailing the bravery of police officers, but said community trust in forces was falling.

She announced a new national standard was being developed "to ensure all members of the public are treated equally".

"Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed," she told the conference.

But failures have allowed some people to "whip up" the false narrative that two-tier policing exists, she said.

She added: "Where differential treatment is caused by inconsistencies or a lack of clarity in the law, it falls on the government to remedy that. We write the laws, you enforce them."

Mahmood called for "clear, comprehensive guidance" on police impartiality, which reinforces that officers must apply the law consistently to avoid what she called "motivated actors" whipping up the idea that there's two-tier policing.

The home secretary said that community engagement can mean going to a residents' association meeting and having tea and biscuits - or samosas - but it shouldn't mean engaging with activists pushing an agenda.

"Leave the politics to the politicians," she added. "And we will leave the policing to you."

The home secretary said more needed to be done to tackle inequalities in policing, highlighting the persistently low proportion of black police officers.

However, she noted that some "well-intentioned approaches", such as the Police Anti-Racism Commitment , had "risked undermining confidence in impartial policing".

"As a Muslim home secretary, no one can doubt that equality in policing, and in our forces, matters to me," she said.

"None of us can accept the racism that was repulsively on display at Charing Cross Police station .

"But we must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment.

"To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing "does not mean treating everyone the same."

Another example she pointed to was the situation when police officers were taking part in a Pride march and "not just policing it".

Mahmood said that scenario may have felt "relatively uncommon" in society a decade ago but added: "There is politics in those issues today. It's contested, and the police should not be getting involved."

Talking to journalists after her speech, Mahmood rejected any claims of two-tier policing.

"That is utter complete ridiculous rubbish. That is not what's happening in our police forces.," she said.

In response to Mahmood's announcement, the Conservatives said they had been "calling out unequal treatment for years".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp added: "The home secretary finally admits there is a problem – and we will now hold her to her own commitments to make sure there is real change."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage claimed the home secretary's speech proved there had been two-tier policing, despite her sayng otherwise.

"We said there was two-tier policing. We were called racist," he said.

"The Labour Home Secretary has now admitted it [saying} 'there have been examples of differential treatment'.

Gavin Stephens, chairman of the National Police Chiefs' Council, said police were sometimes put into extraordinarily difficult situations.

"Discretion means that two situations will be dealt [with] differently that on the face of it might be the same," he said.

But he said the reporting of such incidents sometimes did not reflect the "nuance of what's going on".

He added: When we're trying to do difficult things to make improvements, if we make a misstep or a mistake, like in some clumsy language in a guidance document, it's really helpful that we're supported to make progress, and we don't go back to repeat old arguments."

Jo Noakes who leads the College of Policing, the standards-setting body for the police, said it will issue new guidance for officers that will make clear on impartiality in spring.

She said: "Policing must act in a way that maintains public confidence, which is dependent on officers and staff exercising their powers without fear or favour.

"Impartiality cannot be seen in isolation but needs to be considered alongside how policing acts with fairness and inclusion - both in its own ranks and with the public."

Mahmood also used the speech to announce policing in England and Wales would be restructured into about 200 local commands.

She added each area would be around the size of a unitary authority and led by a named commander.

stories.body:
Published 18 November 2026

Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell has criticised media organisations for broadcasting a message from the wife of jailed rapist Russell Brand on his behalf.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence .

The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.

"I was appalled at that [message] and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either," she told LBC on Wednesday.

"It's a platform I don't think should have been amplified, to be honest."

Powell went on to describe Russell Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

She continued: "This is somebody who's been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape."

In a statement, the BBC said the Today programme had played the Laura Brand clip "in error, due to miscommunication within the team", and had since removed it from catch-up service BBC Sounds.

BBC News has asked the other outlets named above for a comment.

ITN News chief executive Ian Rumsey told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show that the company's newsrooms, including ITV News and Channel 4 News, took the decision not to play the video.

He said: "You didn't need to show it. You could discuss, you could describe what it was, and I'm very pleased and proud that every area of ITN chose not to show it at all, and I think that's exactly the right decision."

YouTube said it is aware of the video and investigating, and that Brand's channel on the platform hasn't been able to make money since being suspended from its advert revenue scheme for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy" after allegations against him emerged in 2023. But the channel is still available to view.

Brand's social media accounts on Meta platforms - which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

Earlier this week, Downing Street officials described Brand's message to his followers as "clearly appalling", adding that it was being urgently investigated.

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

A poll of more than 40,000 workers found that a better work-life balance was the main reason people consider leaving their jobs

Work-life balance has become the leading reason why workers consider leaving their jobs, according to a new global workforce survey, as flexibility is valued more than a higher salary despite the cost of living crisis.

A poll of more than 40,000 global workers found that the top reasons for seeking a new role were better balance between professional and private lives, more flexibility over working schedules or remote working opportunities.

International recruitment firm Adecco said it is the first time in the seven years since launching its annual World of Work report that pay has slipped down the rankings.

This suggests people are “increasingly concerned with how work fits into their lives and not just how it rewards them”, the report found, more than six years after Covid overturned many employees’ expectations about their working lives.

“Every company that wants to bring people back to the office struggles with actually implementing these measures to their full extent,” Denis Machuel, the chief executive of the Swiss-headquartered Adecco Group, said. “Companies saying … ‘It’s going to be five days a week’. It doesn’t work.”

This is despite the continuing battle between some employers and their office-based staff over workplace attendance.

UK banking group NatWest became one of the latest firms to toughen up its office attendance requirements in October, when it announced it would end its remote-first policy , ordering 13,000 staff to increase their in-office days to two a week from two a month.

After several years of hiring flexibly on short-term contracts, companies are beginning to recruit more permanent staff again. That is despite global economic uncertainty caused by the Iran war and the US midterm elections, and increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) in many organisations.

“We see permanent recruitment volumes restarting,” said Machuel. “There’s a mindset of saying ‘uncertainty is here to last, I’d better make a decision’.”

However, Adecco found younger employees have different expectations of their careers and are more likely than their older colleagues to switch roles if they are not satisfied, leading to a disconnect between employers and their younger staff.

“We hear a lot of companies being puzzled by young people saying ‘I’ve been six months in the role, now I’m ready for the next’,” Machuel said.

Organisations’ use of AI has also ramped up, as firms expect to automate administrative or repetitive tasks. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of workers globally reported using AI agents at work, compared with 64% in 2025. In the UK, only a slightly lower percentage (72%) of workers said they used AI.

after newsletter promotion

In workplaces where AI is well integrated into existing workflows, employees reported saving 20% more time each day than people who said it was less integrated.

The continued rollout of AI also led to a 16% relative decline in employment for young people aged 22 to 25 for roles such as customer service and software development, according to previous tracking.

However, Machuel said some professional firms that cut back on entry-level hires over the past 18 months are now changing course, as the jobs market remains tight.

“They are reopening the base of the pyramid because they realise that you cannot bet on buying experienced people from the market,” he said.

Huang’s exit sharpens debate over US stance towards Beijing; and as outages increase, do you get the feeling nothing works?

This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here .

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a plane back from Web Summit in Lisbon. Today in tech, we’re discussing the implications of Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the recent spate of failures in critical infrastructure in everything from Microsoft Outlook accounts to air traffic control to copper wires in routers.

Nvidia’s CEO exit becomes a political proxy war

The chief executive officer of what once was the most valuable company in the world resigned on Thursday. Jensen Huang ’s departure from chipmaker Nvidia after news broke he had at least three affairs – one with an executive at the datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China; others with his own employees – has already cost his company hundreds of billions in stock market value. It may cost the world economy much more. Nvidia is central to the AI boom both as chipmaker and lender.

We’ll know more about the company’s path forward later on Tuesday when it reports its quarterly earnings. Executives, especially interim CEO Colette Kress, will face investors’ questions about the post-Huang era.

The scandal has highlighted divisions among two heavyweights within the Trump administration, each fighting for the US to take their preferred stance toward China. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is accusing the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , of failing to curb sales by Nvidia that contravened export controls.

Here’s how the business of Megaspeed worked, which is what the two secretaries are warring over. Nvidia is barred from selling advanced chips to China. Megaspeed, where the alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, would buy Nvidia chips from its base in south-east Asia, installing them in datacenters in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. From there, it would lease or sell them to Chinese clients.

Lutnick has pushed to allow more trade with China, particularly where his family business, Cantor Fitzgerald, is concerned . Bessent argues for a more hawkish posture and more restrictions.

The question is what will happen next. I think the scandal will result in harsher export controls on China , given that Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in contravention of US export controls. Monday morning already saw the Trump administration moving to tighten them.

Who’s going to win? Both men are traveling with Donald Trump to China this week. I’ll be listening to the president’s remarks for clues about which policy path he’ll choose.

Resignation provokes debate over role of Nvidia founder

Had Jensen Huang amassed too much influence before his downfall? The Nvidia founder seemed indispensable to the success of his company until the very moment he left.

Elon Musk and a host of other Silicon Valley power players argued over the weekend that Huang was irreplaceable and that he should be reinstated. Trump said the same thing on Monday: “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return … I would certainly not mind seeing that.” They’re certainly right that it will be difficult to find another businessman like him.

The possibility may be remote. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a return to Nvidia with allies, à la Sam Altman’s firing and rehiring at OpenAI. The next day, the FT reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was not considering reinstating Huang.

Critics of Silicon see Huang’s departure as a repudiation of the myth of the all-knowing, all-important company founder.

“This week is seeing a long-overdue reckoning for the genius-founder business model,” said Alison Taylor, associate professor at New York University’s business school. Gil Durán , a strident critic of Silicon Valley, made a similar point during a panel organized in response to the news, as did Carissa Véliz, a philosophy professor at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI.

Nvidia’s fate is the highest-profile example I’ve ever seen of “ key man risk ”. Companies heavily reliant on the brilliance of one person – usually a man – or a small group of executives often notify their investors that, if said vital person goes out of commission, the business will suffer. Companies with more diffuse responsibility hedge against that possibility but become more bureaucratic, leading many Silicon Valley companies to operate with as few employees as necessary for as long as possible.

“Relying on the judgment and ethics of one person, no matter how brilliant, is always a catastrophically bad idea, and powerful CEOs are particularly vulnerable because they tend to be surrounded by people that only say yes to them,” Taylor said.

Huang had made no succession plan to speak of, though that may be a failure of Nvidia’s board as much as his own. Huang reportedly managed about 60 people, meaning there are unlikely to be successors who have ascended through the ranks. Judging by Nvidia’s stock price, this approach to management worked until the key man himself hit a crisis.

Cast in another light, though, Huang’s tenure looks like the best case of a founder assuming the role of longtime CEO. He presided over Nvidia for more than 30 years, and shepherded it from gaming chip company to vital cryptocurrency supplier to the keystone of the AI boom. Its wares are considered the cream of the crop, so incomparable that they are the target of international espionage operations and so valuable that the company forecast $100bn in quarterly revenue .

The feeling that nothing works

A spate of failures indicates critical systems are crumbling as we speak, particularly in the US. Banks, planes, email accounts and boats all crashing – it feels like nothing is working and everything is broken.

Late last week, an outage of Microsoft Outlook started that would balloon into millions having no access to their email or other critical services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday. It also issued an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, instead saying in an initial report that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections and insufficient server capacity sparked the outage.

The day after the Microsoft outage began, the US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the country because of a malfunctioning communication system. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, attributed the stoppage to “a contractor doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber”. The FAA, he said on Saturday, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”.

Copper wires downing all US flights in the year 2026, when we have thousands of self-driving cars on the roads and rockets landing in giant machine arms ? The discrepancy gives credence to the axiom by the author William Gibson: “The future is already here – it’s just not evenly distributed.”

Also on Friday, an oil tanker collided with a passenger cruise ship on the Mississippi River. Mercifully, no one was killed . On Sunday, Australian students couldn’t take their final exams because of a tech failure . On Monday, leading US banks reported big outages, primarily JPMorgan Chase. Customers could not access online services such as Zelle, which the bank attributed to an unspecified technical issue. The same day, multiple main airlines reported major outages. United and American Airlines reported problems that delayed flights across the country, though they were resolved within hours of being announced.

These outages are not, by the available evidence, connected, nor do we know they are the result of cyber-attacks or rogue AI. Still, there is a feeling in the air of old systems breaking down and a strong impulse to blame someone. Are the disruptions the result of old systems’ transition to the new? The onslaught of cyber-attacks brought on by AI models’ advanced hacking capabilities?

I don’t know what’s causing so much mayhem. The absence of a unified explanation in the face of so many similar incidents remains maddening. We’ll have to sit with the uncertainty until answers arrive.

In the meantime, we have Stephen King’s speculation for solace: “The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”

High-stakes hearing comes in wake of resignation from Nvidia after alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who chair the committees, said in a press release. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”

The three congressmen chair the foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the intelligence committee of the House of Representatives, respectively. On 12 November, they had signed a letter warning Huang that he could face a subpoena if he did not agree to the closed-door meeting.

Nvidia chips are key to powering the artificial intelligence boom. The Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after allegations of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees surfaced.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been Megaspeed International’s executive director. The Singapore-based cloud computing company has bought nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. The company said Alice Huang stepped down in 2025.

Megaspeed ultimately facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, i n violation of US export controls. On Friday, Malaysia stated that they were investigating whether the company diverted advanced AI ships to other countries.

A recent joint Department of Commerce and Department of Justice letter, stated that the Department of Commerce , under its secretary, Howard Lutnick, first started an investigation in Megaspeed on 2024 for potential export control violations. The justice department, led by the attorney general, Todd Blanche, took over in 2025.

In his first remarks since his resignation, Jensen Huang said on Thursday he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley tech giants, along with 165,000 signatories to an open letter, have called for his reinstatement. Trump has also signaled his openness for the disgraced tech CEO’s return.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
stories.summary: There is hope his Neets report has created a case on benefits which MPs can back, writes political editor Chris Mason.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Alan Milburn's proposals to help young people who are neither learning nor earning would reduce benefits for some young people but aim to get them jobs in the long run

Published 18 November 2026

The prime minister describes Alan Milburn's report on jobs, training and benefits for young people as a "watershed moment".

In so doing, he is accepting Milburn's case for change and taking on the task of delivering it. Were ministers to actually manage that, it would amount to one of the most significant shake-ups of the welfare state in its history.

But the proposed timeframe for this stretches to a decade, which is another geological era in political terms, at least two general elections away.

Milburn is a deft operator. From a round of morning television and radio interviews, to addressing the cabinet, to releasing his report into the wild, he was still out and about on Tuesday evening in Westminster persuading, charming and cajoling those possibly in need of all three.

And this former MP, still every inch the politician, has an ongoing role - appointed the chairman of the government's new Youth Opportunities Unit.

The new job, which will report directly to Andy Burnham, is about tying together the myriad different aspects of change he is suggesting, involving multiple government departments.

And yes, it does mean a 68-year-old bloke becomes an early beneficiary of new employment prospects for the young.

But that glib observation apart, there is a hope that Milburn has gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reforms they can endorse. Or, to put it more bluntly, one not grounded in a specific objective to make benefits cuts to make the sums add up elsewhere.

Plus, him hanging around perhaps means he can be a useful lightning conductor for any forthcoming angst on Labour's benches – as having persuaded them of the big picture mission, the gritty reality of implementing it begins to take shape.

Burnham promises to 'move quickly' on Neets report Published 23 hours ago

Watch: What's in the Milburn review? Published 2 days ago

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 2 days ago

The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis Published 2 days ago

As the prime minister puts it in an interview in the Times , external , the government wants to offer "a new social contract" for "the let-down generation".

And he tells the newspaper that the initial upfront cost of around £500m, for employment support in 2027-28, will come from existing government budgets, which will mean cuts to other things elsewhere in government.

"I've asked the cabinet to reprioritise," he said.

Crucially, if you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, many of the decisions around whether or not to press ahead with these ideas will be up to the devolved governments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.

From the government at Westminster's perspective, the focus now will be drawing up the specific plans for implementing Milburn's ideas, having accepted the broad thrust of his argument.

A white paper will follow in the new year, and then legislation.

What we don't know yet and will be crucial to the next stage of this debate, is precisely who will be the perceived winners and losers, at least in the short term, of the proposed changes.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told me that "those with the most severe and lifelong disabilities where work is not a realistic prospect" should, as Milburn suggests, "get more support than they receive at the moment". But how will those in this category be defined?

McFadden also told me that for some of those facing "extra costs" associated with their circumstances "there will be an extra cost benefit that will make at least a contribution towards that".

Again, how will those in this category be defined?

There is too an emerging political argument, following remarks from Alan Milburn already seized upon by the Conservatives, that decisions taken by Labour in its first few years in power have made a difficult situation harder still for young people looking for work.

On page 66 of his report , external , Milburn says the Employment Rights Act 2025 "could have major implications at a time when the youth labour market is already weak".

Interestingly, on this point, the prime minister is willing to push back, telling BBC Breakfast that "there is a balance to be struck".

"It is important to consider on the other side of this that the more you strengthen employment security, that can create more durable jobs that young people are more likely to stay in," he says. "We're going to consider all of this in the round."

The big decisions, then, now sit on the prime minister and the work and pensions secretary's desks.

In accepting the magnitude of Milburn's diagnosis and proposed treatment, they are tacitly accepting too that it is their responsibility to deliver – or at least begin to deliver – on much of what he suggests.

Their success or otherwise will matter to this generation of young people and those that will follow – and to the sustainability of the benefits system in the years ahead.

stories.body:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy

I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.

On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.

The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.

All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.

A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.

“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”

Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.

Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.

Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.

A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.

The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.

“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”

China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”

The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.

The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”

For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”

For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

stories.title: Voters Reject ALPRs and Surveillance Tech at the Ballot Box
stories.summary: Do automated license plate readers (ALPRs) have any place in our communities? That question has been a hot topic in city council meetings , community conversations , and news coverage around the country for months. This past election day, a couple of U.S communities took it further: to the ballot. And overwhelmingly, voters decided that, no, these devices should not be deployed on our streets. We agree! In Maine, the coastal community of York voted to remove the town’s existing ALPR cameras and require that any future proposed installations receive voter approval before proceeding. The local initiative ended up on the ballot after constituents gathered enough signatures on a citizens’ petition for a local ordinance. On Election Day, nearly three-quarters of York voters supported the ban. Thousands of miles away, voters in League City, Texas also voted against allowing the local police department to continue use of ALPR cameras. That vote was formally approved on November 17, which began a 72-hour window to remove the cameras. Since the election, the cameras have been “bagged” or covered to prevent the collection of data. At least one city also decided to expand protections afforded to their residents when it comes to the use of surveillance technology. In Pflugerville, Texas, Proposition B passed , now requiring that the City Charter be amended to include “protections governing the collection, use, retention, and oversight of data, facial recognition, and surveillance technologies.” It also requires “a responsible artificial intelligence framework.” While every municipality has different rules for how to get a local ordinance placed on the ballot, banning use and securing the removal of surveillance tools locally is a powerful way of protecting your community against devices and data collection that goes far beyond your town lines. Surveillance is a choice, not a mandate, and our communities have the power to refuse it. EFF has supported local communities around the country over the last few years in advocating against the procurement of surveillance technologies in their cities, counties, and states. These victories at the ballot box and in city councils show that when mass surveillance is presented as a policy choice, not a technical necessity, communities can and do reject it. stories.summary: Software patents are mostly vague, hard to define, and widely abused. Most tech patent lawsuits aren’t filed by companies that make real products. They’re filed by patent trolls, companies that acquire patents to extract payments through litigation and legal threats. A patent on one feature of a smartphone shouldn’t give the patent owner the power to threaten the existence of the entire product line. But that is exactly the leverage patent trolls want—and the current administration is helping them to get it. In two recent patent cases, Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung and Collision Communications v. Samsung, the Justice Department and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office have asked courts to make it easier for patent owners to get injunctions. These are judicial orders that can force companies to stop selling products or remove features from them, rather than simply pay monetary damages. The threat of an injunction can pressure a company to pay far more than what a patent is actually worth. In 2006, NTP Inc., a patent holding company with no products of its own, was able to pressure BlackBerry manufacturer Research in Motion Ltd. to pay a $612 million settlement when it was on the verge of an injunction. Protection Against Patent Trolls In May 2006, the Supreme Court rejected the practice of granting permanent injunctions almost automatically after a finding of patent infringement. In eBay v. MercExchange , the high court held that patent owners must satisfy the same tough requirements that plaintiffs in non-patent cases must meet to get a permanent injunction. After eBay, patent owners had to show “irreparable harm,” that they can’t be adequately compensated by money, that the “balance of hardships” favors the plaintiff, and, critically, that an injunction would not harm the “public interest.” At EFF, we celebrated eBay v. MercExchange as a major win for internet users. More than twenty years ago, we saw that software patents were going to be a disaster—not just for small companies (which they are), but for freedom of expression online. stories.title: The Paramount-Warner Brothers Deal Could Usher in Another Age of Lost Media
stories.summary: There are all sorts of reasons to be against the merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers-Discovery. There's the obvious problem of increasing concentration in the already pretty-concentrated film and TV industry. People have problems with Paramount's owner Skydance interfering with its news coverage and late night comedy . But one of the biggest is the way we are losing choice and access to information and culture. In the context of the digital world, there are two major problems with these mega mergers. One, as we've said in the past, is that it further degrades the already awful state of mainstream streaming services. In short, by increasing the amount of legacy content under their control, major studios don't have to invest in either new content or well-engineered services to get users. Plus, they can pool the data they have on users together in an increasing assault on consumer privacy. A monthly subscription and more information about your habits and interests? Win-win for them. Another problem is the disappearing of content. In the digital era, there should be no more lost media. Making and storing copies of media is easier and cheaper than it ever has been. The idea of the persistence of content online has become the adage "the internet never forgets." However, since more and more media is locked behind subscription services under the control of fewer and fewer companies—and as physical copies, or even just digital copies that are actually owned by consumers also vanish—access to our common culture is at risk. Incentives to take information and media offline should raise huge red flags. Unfortunately, they are multiplying. stories.title: European Commission Plan to Give Frontex Trusted Flagger Status Is A Threat to Free Speech
stories.summary: EFF and 27 other human rights organizations called on the European Commission today to retract a dangerous proposal granting its border agency Frontex power to request that national authorities issue takedown orders for social media content and giving Frontext “trusted flagger” status under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU regulation governing online platforms and content moderation in the region. The extraordinarily improper proposal not only disregards the provisions of the DSA but also places a mechanism of enforcement overreach in the hands of a law enforcement agency that has failed to safeguard people against serious human rights violations at EU borders. Under the proposal , Frontex has the power to “monitor publicly accessible social media content, detect developments relevant to external border management, and support action against illegal online content linked to border-security risks.” Granting Frontex trusted flagger privileges on top of its existing mandate risks creating a powerful tool for over-enforcement, stifling the free expression of migrants, asylum seekers, and other marginalized groups. We warned the Commission of these risks in a letter . The DSA is supposed to make online platforms more accountable and protect users’ fundamental rights, not give the EU power to sic its border police on people for exercising their right to free expression. EFF and other rights organizations have for years sounded alarms about potential abuse under the DSA’s trusted flagger provision, which gives “Digital Services Coordinators” the ability to award entities—including law enforcement agencies—a privileged channel to alert online platforms about illegal content. We’ve taken the firm position that law enforcement cannot be trusted to properly flag illegal content. In July, we told the Commission that giving law enforcement trusted flagger status could undermine fundamental rights and said that police agencies like Frontex should not be made trusted flaggers. The EU proposal gives Frontex decision-making power over free expression that is not envisaged under the DSA. First, content removal orders can only be issued by relevant national authorities. The DSA does not foresee a role for entities like Frontex to request such orders.
